The practitioner can state which use can start, identify an uncovered peak, data restriction, assessment requirement, checking burden or fallback, and decide whether to revise the arrangement or report the remaining gap.

Establishing competence, access, peak demand, handoffs and privacy conditions has a cost. Some designs remain infeasible. A class arrangement may still need to be adapted for a person. To establish learning, compare the person’s performance across suitable occasions and account for the help they received.

### HCD.7:10 - Rationale

Feasibility depends on whether the required contribution can reach its recipient from a capable, authorized provider within the available time and capacity, under the applicable access and consequence limits. A title and an aggregate budget do not establish all those relations.

Distinguishing intended, permitted, available and received help supports design and later interpretation. Budgeting the necessary human checks makes their workload and authority visible. If a missing contribution is still needed, a precise account lets the practitioner compare obtaining it with building it, or seek a particular result from the responsible source.

### HCD.7:11 - SoTA-Echoing

**Which evidence shows that a developmental activity can obtain the support it needs within its time, capacity and authority limits?**

Brooks and colleagues’ 2024 qualitative study of learning-health-system communities ([`SOC-05`](https://doi.org/10.1002/lrh2.10412)) identifies distinct contributions from participants, platforms, facilitation, leadership and resources. Its qualitative findings help identify arrangement conditions. A claim that the arrangement caused capability development needs separate evidence. Matsuo and Tsukube’s 2020 cognitive-apprenticeship review ([`SOC-02`](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijme.2020.100417)) distinguishes modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection and exploration. Their sequence and transfer to a workplace depend on the particular use. Sections 4.2–4.5 apply those distinctions when allocating contributions and checking proposed service.

A provider title and total hours are cheap to obtain and can contribute to planning. They leave distinct questions about competence, individual work, peak load, access, privacy, assessment independence and fallback. Examine the conditions that the receiving use needs and the initial information leaves open.

Tullis, Goldstone and Hanson’s 2015 motor-task experiment ([`COG-11`](https://doi.org/10.1080/00222895.2015.1008686)) found that the timing of assistance mattered and that better assisted practice performance could be followed by poorer unassisted performance. Select help or fading from the demands of the actual work. Wiese, Kilty and Bennett’s 2018 clinical realist synthesis ([`SOC-03`](https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13655)) relates supervised participation and graduated access to task risk, trust, learner position and service pressure. Other settings need their own governance conditions. Dell’Acqua and colleagues’ field experiment ([`AI-03`](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2025.21838)) supports independent error checking under the tasks and model conditions examined. Sections 4.3–4.7 use these findings to distinguish support conditions, human checks and observations with changed support.

Checking contributions in their required windows can cost more than planning from provider names and totals. Its value lies in the competence, timing, authority, privacy, checking and fallback questions it resolves. Revisit the affected part if a task, provider, capacity window, access rule, AI condition, evidence use or source changes its grounds. A lower-effort check can suffice if it establishes those conditions.

### HCD.7:12 - Relations

- **`HCD.2`** identifies the contributions and access proposed by a programme candidate. HCD.7 establishes which are available for the intended use and where a proposed contribution still lacks support.
- **`HCD.5`:** supplies Method-specific provider, support, task, risk, and evidence needs.
- **`HCD.6`:** supplies task materials, permitted help, criteria, feedback opportunities, and domain-provider requirements.
- **`HCD.8`** compares obtaining or building a required contribution still unavailable from the provider or environment. It helps arrange any needed preparation and establish performance where the intended use requires it. HCD.7 can use an existing qualified contribution directly.
- **`HCD.9`:** uses the enabled arrangement and records help actually received, feedback delivered, corrections, and provider failures during practice.
- **`HCD.10`:** may change support across practice episodes for a stated development or evidence purpose; the revised arrangement must remain feasible.
- **`HCD.11`–`HCD.13`** help interpret evidence of supported or independent performance, transfer, retention and changes in support. HCD.7 supplies the availability conditions relevant to those claims.
- **`HCD.14`:** may revise only the affected support assumption or programme component from compatible evidence.
- **Learning-product practices:** can specify concrete materials, interactions, and schedules; publication or access does not establish provider competence or service operation.
- **Organization, operations, platform, privacy, safety, legal, clinical, employment, accessibility, provider, and target-domain practices:** retain their own capacity, authority, competence, data, risk, and correctness decisions.

### HCD.7:End

## HCD.8 - Obtain or Build Missing Human Capability-Development Support with Bounded Recursion

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner capability-building pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.8:0 - Use This When

Use this pattern when HCD.7 or an equivalent assessment identifies a contribution a development activity needs and cannot currently obtain. An assessor may lack the ability to distinguish a protected error, a practice environment may lack safe reset, or a provider may be unable to supply a required result in time.

To return a **bounded operating development arrangement**, obtain the missing contribution from a qualified provider or build it, and establish representative operation under the required access, timing, capacity, authority and consequence conditions. Use applicable evidence of that operation where it already exists. If the task asks for a comparison, return the supported routes and their conditions. If operation remains unestablished, identify any useful preparation and what remains unsupported.

Start with the task the provider would perform and the conditions on which that contribution depends. A qualified provider or environment already available may meet the need. If alternatives still need comparison, compare ways to obtain the contribution with ways to build it. Establish what would show it operating when the receiving use needs that judgement.

Use HCD.7 to assess availability and arrange existing contributions. Use the relevant organization, platform, safety, privacy, legal, technical, domain or operations practice for a contribution it must establish, create or authorize. HCD.8 can use that result. Evidence of human learning concerns the person’s performance.

#### HCD.8:0.1 - Working Terms

| Name in this pattern | What it denotes |
| --- | --- |
| missing development contribution | The exact provider, assessment, environment, access, coordination, or support result that an HCD.7 arrangement needs but cannot currently obtain under its required conditions. |
| provider target task | The concrete work a provider must perform to supply that contribution, including recipient, input, output, criteria, protected errors, support, timing, and authority. It is different from the learner's later-Work target. |
| obtain route | Use of an existing capable provider or environment when the evidence supports its fit, availability and operation for the contribution. |
| build route | Preparation or change intended to enable a person, group, organization, tool, service or environment to supply the missing contribution. The relevant practice establishes technical or domain correctness. Authorizations come from the holders of those rights. |
| operating test | A representative enactment in which the intended provider or environment supplies the exact contribution under material service conditions, with observable criteria, timing, handoffs, and failure signals. |
| blocking dependency | A missing provider or enabling result without which the selected route cannot supply or operate the required contribution. |
| recursive build question | Applied to a blocking dependency, which result is missing, could an existing source supply it, what might have to be built and what evidence would establish the required operation? |
| bounded operating development arrangement | A provider or environment contribution established in use under stated conditions, with its dependencies, access, capacity, authority, operating evidence, fallback or safe stop and limits for HCD.7. Identify who supplied the contribution, who received it and what each was observed doing. A learning effect requires separate evidence. |

Read backward from the required contribution to the first unsupported result, if there is one. If a necessary result remains unsupported, establish how it could be supplied. Stop when the evidence answers the receiving question or when a specific gap prevents further progress.

### HCD.8:1 - Problem Frame

A development design can fail after its activities are selected because the arrangement itself cannot do the work. The available teacher may explain the topic but be unable to judge the target-domain error. Two assessors may reach different decisions from the same answer. A simulated environment may exist but lack safe reset or the required configuration. A platform may contain the materials but not deliver the feedback interval promised by the programme.

More training, documentation or technology can leave the required contribution unavailable. A provider may finish preparation and still fail the target task. A functional environment may be unavailable at peak time. A new guide may leave assessors disagreeing about the same criterion.

Start with the missing result, use a qualified available route when it suffices, or compare feasible ways to obtain or create the result. Follow the dependencies of a route the work needs to assess or put into operation. To claim operating availability, use evidence of the contribution in representative operation.

### HCD.8:2 - Problem

“Train the trainers,” “create a lab,” “add mentors” and “install a platform” can describe possible interventions. Each leaves open which provider task or service condition is missing and which result would satisfy it.

A dependency map can expand indefinitely if every provider or tool is treated as requiring another support programme. Trace the relation that blocks the specified result. Accept a qualified available contribution as the end of that branch.

Materials, credentials, reserved hours or configured software can establish preparation. An observed rehearsal may also establish representative operation if it supplies the required contribution to its recipient under the service conditions. Match the evidence to the particular claim.

### HCD.8:3 - Forces

- Obtaining an existing qualified provider can be fast, while fit, availability, independence, access, and continuity still need evidence.
- Developing a provider can preserve local knowledge and future capacity, while it consumes time and may miss the present programme window.
- Building an environment can make representative practice possible, while safety, data, configuration, reset, maintenance, and authorization remain direct-owner results.
- Standard preparation makes provider work more comparable, while a script can conceal whether the provider can handle a changed case or dispute.
- A recursive dependency view can expose the real bottleneck, while following every imaginable dependency creates delay and false structure.
- Representative operation can establish service under the task, provider, load and period observed. A design describes the service expected under proposed conditions.
- A provider may use help that the intended service permits. Claims about independent performance or persistence after support changes require evidence under those conditions.
- HCD can coordinate a missing development contribution, while domain, employment, safety, legal, privacy, platform, organization, and operations owners retain their own decisions.

### HCD.8:4 - Solution

Start with a specific gap established by HCD.7 or an equivalent assessment. Identify the provider’s task, the service conditions and whether a qualified source can supply the contribution in time. Where the task needs a comparison, compare feasible ways to obtain the contribution with the smallest build that could supply it. Follow the dependencies that affect the route being assessed or used. To return an operating contribution, establish representative performance under the required conditions using suitable existing evidence or a needed operating test.

#### HCD.8:4.1 - Bind One Missing Contribution

Establish the following facts to the extent needed for the requested result.

1. the learner, class, programme, practice, or evidence use that is blocked;
2. the missing contribution, recipient, required time, output form, criteria, protected errors, and consequence boundary;
3. what the availability assessment has already established about providers, access, capacity, constraints and fallback;
4. the sources of technical, domain, competence, safety or privacy evidence and the holders of any permission or decision the route requires; and
5. the observation or operating evidence that would establish the missing contribution for HCD.7, including any applicable result already available.

For an instructor, identify the work they must perform for the recipient. For an environment, identify the function it must supply and the access, timing and operating conditions in which it must work.

#### HCD.8:4.2 - Compare Obtaining with Building

Use an established route if it meets the task. If the available routes leave the required contribution unmet, try to construct a workable route by combining suitable provision or building the missing part. Compare feasible candidates on the following conditions when the task needs a comparison. If none fits, identify the obstacle.

| Comparison position | Obtain an existing contribution | Build the missing contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| result fit | Evidence that the provider or environment can supply the exact result | Target task, proposed change and grounds that it could produce the result |
| time and window | Onboarding, contracting, access, calibration, and actual availability | Preparation, practice, correction, retest, installation, validation, and ramp-up |
| burden and risk | Search, handoff, confidentiality, continuity, dependency, and switching burden | Development effort, supervision, failure exposure, maintenance, and displaced work |
| authority and independence | Permission, accountability, assessment independence, and domain legitimacy | Who can authorize, judge, and operate the created contribution |
| operating evidence | Representative sample or observed service under the intended conditions | Evidence of representative operation after preparation or change, including an applicable test already performed |
| continuation | Renewal, backup, transfer, or replacement condition | Maintenance, refresh, supervision, fallback, and smallest reopen condition |

Compare the routes for the required contribution, including timing, burden, risk, continuity and evidential conditions. Assess which alternatives remain after eliminating those dominated on the relevant criteria. Return the remaining feasible route or routes and any unresolved trade-offs. Establish any programme choice or authorization separately.

#### HCD.8:4.3 - Specify the Provider or Environment Target Task

For a human provider, define the work they must perform, including what it requires and what is already known.

- representative inputs and cases;
- required explanation, feedback, assessment, preparation, coordination, or specialist output;
- criteria and protected errors supplied by the target domain;
- permitted references, tools, AI, colleague or supervisor help;
- required response time, volume, handoff, independence, and authority; and
- available performance evidence, uncertainty and any preparation, correction or further operating observation that the intended use still requires.

Use HCD methods for an open question about a human provider’s ability. For a service, platform, tool or environment, establish the needed technical, safety, privacy, access or operating result using the appropriate evidence. If another contributor or authority is required, identify the result to obtain from them.

#### HCD.8:4.4 - Expose Only Blocking Dependencies

Read backward from the missing contribution. An assessor may need a calibrated key from a specialist who needs an approved test result to supply it. A practice environment may need isolated data and reliable reset. Use a qualified result already available. Where the dependency remains open, identify what would close it and seek the contribution if a capable source is needed and available.

A.1.STM’s plain long-mantra map helps when the builder chain is not established. Keep the final contribution visible, identify the supported dependencies and locate any result that still lacks support. Use E.18.NET when the work requires independently identified transformation-flow structures and evidence of particular relations across their boundaries. Naming two flows or drawing an arrow between them does not establish that a cross-boundary relation occurred.

Stop recursion when:

- an already qualified and available contribution satisfies the dependency;
- a direct owner returns the required result under compatible conditions;
- the selected route can proceed without the optional dependency; or
- an unsupported dependency is identified with its consequence, any known source and what would permit work to resume.

Build or change a provider or environment when it is a justified way to obtain the missing contribution. Trace a node further only if its contribution to a route being assessed or used remains unsupported.

#### HCD.8:4.5 - Prepare and Enact the Smallest Build

For a chosen build, select preparation suited to the provider-task gap. Examples include modelling, guided practice, criterion comparison, supervised access, a safe test environment, a calibrated key, tool configuration or rehearsal for a dispute. Keep any observed starting attempt with the support the provider received, along with other applicable evidence of entry performance, so a claim about prior competence can be distinguished from performance after preparation.

For human practice, give feedback on a specific action and obtain another attempt when correction or additional evidence is needed. For a claim about an operating environment or service, establish whether the changed function performs under the relevant access and load conditions, including how a failure is signalled and how the service recovers where these affect the required use. Use qualified evidence or obtain the operating result from the responsible practice. Report materials, reservations or completed instruction as preparation unless they also establish the claimed operation.

#### HCD.8:4.6 - Run an Operating Test

Use evidence of the intended provider or environment supplying the contribution in a safely bounded representative use. If further evidence is needed and attainable, run a permitted test under the material service conditions. Identify the following details when they affect the conclusion.

1. the provider, recipient, task, configuration, support, and the sources or decision holders relevant to that use;
2. the input, output, criteria, protected errors, timing, volume, handoffs, and access conditions;
3. the first operating result, any disagreement or failure, any feedback or correction, and the result of a repeat if one occurred;
4. the observed load, latency and consequences, and any escalation or fallback needed or exercised; and
5. the exact claim supported, its limits, and the smallest change that reopens it.

Repeating a memorized case may establish execution of that procedure. If the task requires discrimination, adaptation or dispute handling, establish it from performance under relevant variation. Use an additional case if the available evidence does not settle the claim. Match assistance to the intended service and require unsupported performance when that is part of the provider’s task.

The evidence can establish the contribution delivered to identified recipients under the observed conditions. To extend the claim to other learners, service loads, a whole programme, transfer, retention or learning effects, obtain evidence relevant to that additional claim.

#### HCD.8:4.7 - Return the Obtained or Built Contribution or Exact Stop

Return the result and the conditions under which a recipient can use it.

| Result position | What to return for the requested use |
| --- | --- |
| contribution boundary | Missing contribution, affected development use and recipient, provider task, conditions, consequences and applicable sources or decision holders |
| route comparison | Feasible obtaining or building routes, criteria for their fit, burden, time, risk, authority, continuity and evidence of operation, with remaining trade-offs |
| dependency boundary | Supported inputs, any remaining blocking dependency, sources used and where the search stopped |
| preparation | Proposed or completed preparation or change, its conditions and limits, including the support, practice, feedback or correction that matters to the claimed result |
| operating evidence | Representative service, its conditions, observed result, criteria, timing and load. Identify disputes, corrections or fallback where they affect the claim, and any observation still missing. |
| disposition | A supported comparison or proposal, `qualified existing contribution obtained`, `bounded operating development arrangement`, `preparation only` or `exact unsupported dependency` |
| continuation | The intended HCD.7 use, any further operating evidence or provider result needed, applicable maintenance or fallback, and conditions for reconsideration |

Give HCD.7 the contribution or identified limit it needs, with the applicable conditions. Evidence about provider preparation, operation of the service, receipt by a learner, the learner’s performance and the effects on learning each supports its own claim.

#### HCD.8:4.8 - Recognition and Assurance

**Recognition.** Use HCD.8 when a development activity lacks a specified contribution and you need to compare ways of obtaining or creating it, or to make one of those ways work. Establish what adequate operating evidence already exists and which result is missing.

**Assurance.** Match the evidence to the claimed result. For operating availability, establish the provider task, relevant domain criteria, supporting dependencies, applicable authority and representative performance under the material conditions. For a choice between routes, use evidence of their fit, time, consequences and burden. A prepared asset or completed course establishes preparation. To claim delivery or successful operation, establish that contribution separately.

#### HCD.8:4.9 - What Changes in Practice

Identify the missing contribution, whether an existing provider can supply it and what the provider or environment must do. Trace any unresolved dependency that could prevent the required operation. Establish what performance HCD.7 could rely on and where work must stop if the dependency cannot be met.

### HCD.8:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.8:5.1 - Calibrate Assessors on Three Contrasting Answers

The availability check found that assessors could not apply the engineering-case criteria consistently. They need to judge short answers against the specified requirement and evidence, retain supported parts, distinguish a sound limited proposal from a resource error or justified request, and resolve disagreements within the final-week assessment window.

For preparation, the assessors compare three answers.

| Case answer | Required assessor judgement |
| --- | --- |
| The report matches HW3/FW8/SCHED2, mandatory checks are confirmed, and 24 test hours are available. The learner proposes ten changes in three homogeneous batches, requiring 23 hours, and states that two of the twelve requested changes remain in the queue. | Supported bounded proposal; evidence applicability, resource limit, and queue consequence are preserved. |
| The same data are supplied, but the learner promises twelve changes because batching is faster. | Unsupported: twelve changes require 27 hours, exceeding the 24-hour limit. |
| The changed report does not identify the tested firmware, and the learner asks which version was tested before relying on it for FW8. | Justified missing-information return. The same refusal would be incomplete when the first row's full compatible report is present. |

Assessors first judge independently. They locate any disagreement in the requirement, answer fragment and supplied evidence. A qualified specialist result or calibrated key can settle the domain question. In a further case only 22 hours are available for the ten changes that need 23. The assessors must reject the promise while preserving criteria that still hold and use the dispute route if a disagreement arises. The judgement and its handoff must fit the service window.

The examples, key and reserved time support preparation. Consistent, timely judgements on the changed case can establish the assessor contribution under those conditions. Judging peak final-week load, performance on other cases or effects on learners requires evidence for the corresponding claim.

#### HCD.8:5.2 - Obtain a Qualified Provider instead of Missing the Window

The programme needs a specialist to check control-logic errors before releasing feedback. It lacks evidence that a local teacher can do that work. Developing a local provider would take six weeks, while the next block starts in ten days. An external specialist is available. The contract and title leave open whether the specialist can meet this task’s criteria and window.

For the external route, establish performance on a representative answer, the protected-error criteria, permitted data access, the forty-eight-hour feedback window and the handoff to the teacher. Check the independence, confidentiality, peak capacity and backup the service requires. If representative operation and the service conditions fit, obtain the contribution and return it to HCD.7. Local provider development can remain a candidate for later use.

#### HCD.8:5.3 - Build a Safe Practice Environment through Direct Owners

A learner needs to practise changing a configuration, and no present environment permits a safe trial. The build needs an isolated dataset, the intended configuration, reset, logging, access control and a bounded failure test. Use the platform and safety results already available and obtain the remaining work or authorizations from the responsible parties.

For the operating test, an authorized participant enters the test environment, makes and reverses the change, triggers the failure signal, restores the baseline and produces the required record within the practice window. If reset fails or production data are still exposed, return the unsupported dependency. A stipulated paper exercise can still support a different learning use under its own conditions.

#### HCD.8:5.4 - Stop the Builder Chain at an Available Contribution

Assessor preparation needs a correct answer key. A domain engineer has compatible evidence, authority and time to supply and defend it. Obtaining that result closes this dependency. If no qualified key can be obtained, identify what remains unsupported and how it affects calibration. Further work needs a way to obtain the result or an authorized change to the route.

### HCD.8:6 - Bias-Annotation

Lenses: **Gov**, **Arch**, **Onto/Epist**, **Prag**, **Did**. The table concerns obtaining or building support for a particular development use.

| Recurring bias | Likely drift | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| train-everyone bias | Every provider is sent through a common programme whether a contribution is missing or not. | Start from an established gap. Use a qualified available contribution that satisfies the dependency. |
| asset-readiness bias | Materials, credentials, allocated hours, or installed software are called operational. | Use evidence of representative operation under the required service conditions. Obtain a further observation if that claim remains open and can be tested. |
| internal-build bias | Local capacity is preferred without comparing delay, evidence, risk, and continuity. | Compare obtain and build routes on the current contribution and window. |
| title-competence bias | Reputation, occupation, or contract is taken as contribution-specific capability. | Establish the provider’s fit and representative operation for the required task. |
| generic-enablement bias | A diagram arrow hides the relation or direct result needed from another owner. | Identify the missing result and which provider work depends on it. Use a qualified source or the relevant practice to establish it. |
| infinite-recursion bias | Every support dependency triggers another full build. | Stop at available qualified contributions, optional branches, or a truthful unsupported result. |
| same-example bias | Repeating the training example is treated as operating discrimination. | Use representative evidence of the required variation or judgement. Use another case if the evidence is missing and a further test is appropriate and available. Otherwise limit the claim to the performance observed. |
| service-effect bias | Successful provider operation is reported as learner capability or programme effectiveness. | Keep provider operation, learner receipt, learner attempt, transfer, and retention separate. |

### HCD.8:7 - Conformance Checklist

- [ ] The missing contribution, blocked use, recipient, conditions, and consequence are explicit.
- [ ] Check whether a qualified existing provider or environment can meet the need before selecting a build.
- [ ] Where routes compete, compare fit, time, burden, risk, authority, continuity and evidence of operation. Identify any condition that excludes a route or keeps its fit uncertain.
- [ ] A human provider's own target task is distinct from the learner's later-Work target.
- [ ] Use qualified evidence for technical, safety, privacy, legal and operating conditions. Establish any required authorization from the applicable rule or decision holder.
- [ ] Trace any dependency that could prevent obtaining the required contribution. Stop at a suitable qualified result, a branch the assessed route can proceed without, or a specific unresolved condition.
- [ ] Identify what was prepared or supplied. If operation is claimed, identify the evidence that establishes it.
- [ ] Support a claim of operation with representative performance under the service conditions that matter, including relevant criteria, load, access, handoff or failure signals.
- [ ] For a claim about discrimination or adaptation, use a case with the relevant variation and evidence that the provider handled it.
- [ ] State the contribution or finding, its grounds and limits, and any remaining fallback, continuation or reconsideration condition the receiving use needs.
- [ ] Return the availability finding the receiving arrangement needs. Distinguish provider preparation, service operation, learner receipt and effects on the learner.
- [ ] Limit claims about observed operation, participation or learner effects to the conditions the evidence supports. State the grounds and assumptions for a proposed route or expected service.

### HCD.8:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “Train the trainers” | The missing provider task and current competent providers disappear behind a generic intervention. | Identify the missing contribution and compare feasible ways to obtain or create it. |
| “The assessor passed the course” | Completion does not show consistent judgement on the target cases. | Use the available target-case attempts, resolve any criterion-level disagreement, and use another representative case if the required judgement remains open and can be tested. |
| “The lab has been designed” | A description does not establish safe access, reset, load, or operation. | Use qualified results about the required access, reset, load and operation. Test remaining conditions when a bounded and permitted trial can establish them. |
| “We bought the platform” | Acquisition does not establish configuration, capacity, provider work, or recipient access. | Establish representative performance of the required service and handoffs, using a new test if sufficient evidence is missing and a test is available. |
| “Every builder needs a builder” | The map becomes an infinite programme rather than a located dependency. | Stop when a compatible qualified contribution is available or return the first unsupported result. |
| “The specialist will enable it” | The specialist's result, timing, authority, and relation to the provider task are hidden. | Use a qualified domain result already available. Ask for the particular missing contribution where necessary, and preserve its conditions. |
| “One calibrated answer is enough” | Memorized reproduction can conceal inability to discriminate a changed case. | If required discrimination or adaptation remains untested, use another representative case when available. Include disagreement handling if it is part of the provider’s task. |
| “The service test proves the programme works” | A provider can operate without establishing learner receipt, learning, transfer or retention. | Keep any observed delivery with its recipient and conditions. Route learner-attempt and effect questions to HCD.9 and HCD.11–HCD.13. |

### HCD.8:9 - Consequences

The practitioner can return the feasible routes and their conditions, obtain an available contribution, build it under specified conditions, or explain which dependency still blocks its use. Evidence of representative operation gives the development programme a basis for relying on that contribution.

Comparing routes, preparing a provider, establishing domain criteria, testing service, resolving disagreements and obtaining external results each take time where needed. Some arrangements therefore remain at the design or preparation stage.

### HCD.8:10 - Rationale

A development arrangement depends on providers and environments that can perform the required work. Naming one identifies a potential contribution. Establish whether it is available and can operate under the conditions that matter. Adopt an existing qualified contribution where it satisfies the need.

Tracing the first unsupported dependency directs work to the contribution that blocks the selected route. Evidence of provider preparation, operation and learner effects answers different questions. HCD.7 can use the operating result while a question about learner effects remains open.

### HCD.8:11 - SoTA-Echoing

**How can a practitioner obtain or build a missing development contribution and establish its operation for the intended use?**

Kraiger and Ford’s 2021 review of workplace instruction ([`COG-10`](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-060109)) distinguishes instructional events, learner activity, learning outcomes, transfer and job performance. It identifies how the learner, design, opportunity, available support and work environment affect the contribution. Matsuo and Tsukube’s 2020 cognitive-apprenticeship review ([`SOC-02`](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijme.2020.100417)) describes modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection and exploration. Each can inform provider preparation where it fits the task. Sections 4.3–4.6 connect the provider’s task, preparation and representative evidence of operation.

A programme can document asset delivery, hours and training completion relatively cheaply. Such records can support claims about preparation. If existing provision and a proposed build compete, compare which can better supply the missing contribution. To rely on a service, establish that the provider handles the required variation under the intended time and load.

Tullis, Goldstone and Hanson’s 2015 laboratory experiment ([`COG-11`](https://doi.org/10.1080/00222895.2015.1008686)) found that assisted practice and later unassisted performance could differ under the conditions studied. Wiese, Kilty and Bennett’s 2018 clinical realist synthesis ([`SOC-03`](https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13655)) relates supervised participation to task risk, trust, learner position and service pressure. Sections 4.3–4.7 use the relevant support and consequence conditions when examining provider work. Other settings require their own evidence of what assistance and authority fit the task.

A.1.STM explains how to trace a required contribution back to its first unsupported dependency and use the relevant subject method. E.18.NET addresses a different question about independently identified transformation-flow structures and relations across their boundaries. A dependency map can locate the result still needed. A claim about a relation across independently identified flows requires evidence of that relation. Evidence that a provider operates comes from the corresponding service work.

Checking a contribution in operation can cost more than recording preparation. The added work is warranted where reliance depends on whether the intended service can function. Reconsider the affected result when a change in the missing contribution, provider task, alternatives, risks, support, operating conditions or evidence affects its grounds. A less costly way of establishing the needed conditions may then suffice.

### HCD.8:12 - Relations

- **`HCD.7`** can identify the missing contribution and the conditions under which the arrangement needs it. A practitioner can use the returned operating contribution or identified limit to reassess availability.
- **`HCD.1`–`HCD.6`** can establish a human provider’s target, current evidence, programme, method or representative practice where one of these is missing.
- Use **`HCD.9`** for a needed provider practice episode and **`HCD.10`** when the work calls for varying practice or support. Keep evidence of that person’s attempt distinct from evidence of providing the service.
- **`HCD.11`–`HCD.14`** help assess a person’s capability or revise the development arrangement using compatible evidence. An operating test can establish the service contribution it observed.
- **`A.1.STM`:** locates the first unsupported builder or enabling dependency while keeping the final development contribution visible and local truths with their subject patterns.
- **`E.18.NET`:** can organize independently identified transformation-flow structures and exact cross-member relations when that stronger network question is live; HCD.8 does not infer them from a build sequence.
- **`A.15.1` and relevant subject practices** help establish performed work, production, capacity, correctness, risk and service operation. Use the relevant practice for a question about legal, accessibility or other service conditions, and obtain any required authorization from its holder. Use the result needed by the selected route.
- **Learning-product practices** can supply provider guides, cases, keys, interfaces and practice materials. Establish provider competence or service operation from the corresponding work.

### HCD.8:End

## HCD.9 - Perform Deliberate Practice with Feedback

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner focused-practice pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.9:0 - Use This When

Use this pattern when a person needs to practise a specific contribution on a representative task with feasible support. Let the learner attempt it and use feedback to correct or retain the action. After a correction, retry the affected requirement. If the supported action was already adequate, obtain another attempt only when the practice question needs one. Keep the episode within its safety conditions.

For coached practice of scientific reasoning during process improvement, §4.10 explains what the learner and coach do and how to give feedback on that reasoning. E.23:4.4.1 describes the process-improvement method being practised. Use evidence about the process, the learner or the coach for the corresponding claim.

A **focused-practice episode result** identifies the task, target action, first response, help received, observed action and result, timing and content of feedback, and the learner’s response. Preserve a first response before answer-bearing help where that distinction matters. Explain why the action changed or was retained, what a needed retry showed, or which difficulty remained. Return the next focus or grounds for stopping. Claims about independent performance, transfer, retention or a causal effect on learning need evidence appropriate to those claims.

The practitioner can identify what the learner contributed and which part of the response came from a teacher, coach, peer, tool or AI. Preserve successful parts of the first attempt. Use any relevant error or uncertainty to select feedback, or confirm why the action already fits. After correction, test the affected requirement. Change the case when discrimination from a memorized answer matters.

If the task omits the target contribution, revise the task using HCD.6. If required feedback or safe access is unavailable, use HCD.7 to arrange an existing contribution, use HCD.8 to obtain or build a missing one, or return the resulting limit. Use HCD.11–HCD.13 for stronger performance, transfer or retention questions. Distinguish the learner’s first response from a demonstration, generated answer or corrected final product.

#### HCD.9:0.1 - Working Terms

| Name in this pattern | What it denotes |
| --- | --- |
| focused-practice episode | One bounded attempt and use of feedback directed at a named action, criterion, error, or discrimination in a representative task. It includes correction followed by a retry when the action needs repair, or reasoned retention when the action is supported. |
| practice focus | The action or relation the learner is trying to change or stabilize under the specified conditions. |
| first attempt | The learner’s initial response under identifiable task, time, source, tool, AI and provider conditions. State the help received and whether the conditions support a claim of independent action. |
| changeable action | An observable selection, explanation, calculation, check, request, refusal, adaptation, enactment, or correction on which feedback can bear. |
| feedback contribution | Information about the task, criterion, observed response, error or next action that reaches the learner in a form and time they can use. Identify its source and the opportunity for use. A score can locate a threshold while leaving the required correction unknown. |
| correction | A learner’s revision of reasoning, action, work product, check, request or explanation in response to feedback. Identify any part supplied by the provider. |
| retry | A subsequent attempt on the affected requirement, with a changed condition when the needed discrimination or adaptation would otherwise remain unobserved. |
| focused-practice episode result | The preserved first attempt, support received, observation, feedback, learner response, any retry or unresolved difficulty, qualification, and next practice focus or stop. |

Here *deliberate practice* means a focused attempt connected to usable feedback. Studies use this name for different arrangements and measures. Section 4.4 helps choose help from what the learner can do with a criterion. Section 11 identifies the findings each source supports and the limits on conclusions about dose, cause, transfer and expertise in a given domain. The name alone settles none of these questions.

### HCD.9:1 - Problem Frame

A record of pages, hours, cases or attendance can establish exposure. To understand a practice episode, establish what the person tried, which help they received, what was observed, whether the feedback arrived in time and what the learner did with it.

A teacher may demonstrate the correct result, a peer may rewrite the response, or AI may generate a correction. The product can improve even when the learner’s own work remains unknown. Preserve the first response and attribute subsequent help and revisions so that later assessment can distinguish independent work, supported work and a supplied answer.

Keep the initial conditions and response. Give the learner information they can use and retry the affected requirement after correction. Feedback can also confirm why an action should be retained. Scope a conclusion about that episode to the performance and help observed.

### HCD.9:2 - Problem

The common shortcut is “more practice.” It treats duration or repetition as the intervention while leaving the target action, provider, information content, task variation, and next observation unspecified. A learner can repeat the same error, receive only a score, or become better at the displayed answer.

Keeping only the corrected product can hide an earlier error, an already sound part of the work and the help used to repair it. A demonstrated or generated solution may then be attributed to the learner.

A third shortcut retests everything after one defect. It wastes already supported results, hides the precise difficulty, and may not fit the promised time. Conversely, passing an unrelated total score can conceal a critical error that still needs correction.

### HCD.9:3 - Forces

- A first response before answer-bearing help can show what the person did independently under the declared conditions. Safety, privacy, irreversible action or other serious consequences may require earlier intervention.
- Immediate feedback can stop error rehearsal, while a safe delay may be needed to observe the learner's initial reasoning.
- A detailed explanation can support a novice, while it can also replace the action the learner was meant to perform.
- Scores can locate a threshold. To act on a score, the learner may need the criterion, the relevant part of the response and the next useful move.
- Reusing a task makes correction economical, while a changed condition may be needed to distinguish understanding from answer memory.
- Preserving passed requirements saves effort, while a new answer can sometimes contradict them and reopen their status.
- Focused repetition can improve performance under the practised conditions. A claim about cause, dose or transfer across domains needs evidence suited to that question.
- Provider and tool support can make practice feasible, while help received must remain visible in the result.

### HCD.9:4 - Solution

Connect a representative task to one practice focus. Preserve the first attempt and its support conditions, compare the action with the criterion and provide feedback when the learner can use it safely. Let the learner correct the affected action or retain one already supported. Ask for a verbal explanation when the target or a remaining question requires it. After correction, retry the affected requirement. After retention, stop unless another observation is needed.

#### HCD.9:4.1 - Bind the Episode before the Attempt

Establish the conditions of the episode.

1. the learner, later-work target, selected development method, representative task and question or decision the episode should inform;
2. the practice focus, observable action, required result, domain criteria, protected errors, and useful uncertainty;
3. the task condition that makes the action necessary and, if the episode tests discrimination or adaptation, one condition that could change the warranted move;
4. the sources, tools, AI, peer, teacher or specialist help permitted, the time available, and the prompts or demonstrations arranged. Use HCD.7 or HCD.8 if a needed contribution still has to be arranged, obtained or built; and
5. the feedback provider, safe intervention point, opportunity to use feedback, retry boundary, and stopping condition.

If a necessary task, criterion, provider contribution, access condition or opportunity to use feedback is missing, identify the blocked part of the episode and what remains possible. Exposure can be reported on its own terms.

#### HCD.9:4.2 - Preserve the First Attempt and Actual Help

When the question concerns independent action, preserve the learner’s response before help supplies that action or answer. Record the conditions that affect interpretation, such as time, sources opened, tools used, prompts or questions, peer or teacher interventions and when the learner received them.

If support belongs to the task, preserve the supported first response and the help received. If safety or another material consequence requires the provider to interrupt, retain the last safe action and the reason for stopping. Distinguish the help planned, permitted, available, received and used where the conclusion depends on it.

#### HCD.9:4.3 - Observe the Changeable Action

Compare the attempt with the criterion and its evidence. Locate the smallest relevant action that helps explain the observed success or difficulty, such as selecting a source, checking a configuration, calculating, requesting help, refusing unsafe work or adapting a decision. State any uncertainty that remains and preserve plausible alternatives when the observation cannot distinguish them.

An error may concern access, support, arithmetic, domain knowledge, fatigue or another condition. Use available evidence to distinguish these explanations where possible. One episode alone seldom supports a claim of a stable deficit. If an open distinction could change the conclusion or intervention, use HCD.3, HCD.6, HCD.7 or relevant domain evidence when that inquiry can help. Otherwise state the supported result and its limit.

#### HCD.9:4.4 - Give Feedback the Learner Can Use

Make the feedback usable for this learner and attempt. Include the following information where it is needed.

- the requirement or criterion and the observed part of the attempt;
- what remains useful and should be preserved;
- any error, uncertainty, missing check, or unsupported relation that needs attention, or the grounds for retaining the action;
- the smallest cue, question, example, explanation, or correction information suitable for the learner and task;
- the next learner action, if one is needed, and the opportunity and any deadline for using the feedback; and
- the provider, channel, timing, support boundary, and any consequence or escalation.

Choose feedback timing from the purpose, risk and error. Intervene at once if continuing would be unsafe, disclose protected data, cause irreversible harm or rehearse a critical error. In a safe task, allow enough of the first response to reveal the learner’s reasoning when that observation matters.

A demonstration, replay, marked interval, changed model or partner response can make the relevant difference accessible. The learner can show its use through a new action, perceptual choice or adjustment. Require words when explaining is part of the target or needed to settle the question. Keep the subject criterion even when a competent performance has no complete verbal description.

A score can locate a threshold and praise can acknowledge effort. For correction, give information that identifies what the learner can change. A full solution can be a useful worked example. If it supplies the current answer, record what the provider supplied. Attribute supported performance to the learner when their subsequent action shows how they used it.

**Choose how the learner will use the criterion.** A model answer or group explanation can leave a learner unsure how it applies to their own attempt. Use available evidence of their comparison. If the ability remains open, preserve the attempt, give the qualified comparison and ask the learner to identify what it supports or changes. Observe what they then do. Merely repeating the model answer does not establish their use of the criterion.

If the learner can apply the comparison, let them compare an attempt with the prepared material, correct it as needed and retry the affected requirement after correction. If they cannot yet locate the decisive difference, arrange a targeted explanation or contrast from a qualified source or provider where the task requires it. HCD.6:4.3 and HCD.6.1 help make the distinction accessible. HCD.7 can help secure a required contribution in time. Return to the whole task when the learner can use the distinction, or identify the support still missing.

Successful use of a supplied explanation establishes what the learner did with that help. To assess detection before help or performance with altered support, use evidence under the corresponding conditions. HCD.10 can help select a needed change. If the learner’s original action was sound and the evidence answers the bounded question, retain it and stop as described in §4.5.

A common explanation can serve several learners while leaving different next steps for each. To establish individual use of the criterion, examine each relevant response and offer targeted help where the shared explanation did not suffice. Include time for that check and help. If the arrangement cannot provide them, narrow the supported claim or identify the missing contribution.


#### HCD.9:4.5 - Use Feedback to Correct or Retain the Action

When feedback identifies an error or unsupported step, let the learner repair it by revising reasoning, action or product, performing a missing check, or giving grounds for stopping. Preserve what the learner did separately from the provider’s input. Retry the affected requirement.

If the action meets its criterion, retain it on the available grounds. For a remaining question the learner might choose a continuation, demonstrate the relation under a changed cue or explain it. A qualified observation can support a correct movement or perceptual choice even before the learner can explain how it was produced. If explanation is the target, it can improve while the practical action stays the same. A score or praise without evidence of the action cannot establish that performance.

Use an adequate existing observation, or choose a further feasible attempt when its attainable contribution warrants the work needed to address a remaining question about stability, adaptation or another requirement. Stop when an already correct attempt and its grounds answer the practice question. Use HCD.11–HCD.13 when the remaining claim concerns performance, transfer or retention. HCD.15:4.2.1 can help derive a learning question from successful work if one is needed.

Use a changed, comparable case if another observation must establish applicability, method selection, adaptation or response to an altered condition. Repeating the same case can check stable execution or a focused correction under the same requirements. Retain previously demonstrated work unless a new response contradicts it or changed conditions affect its use.

If several gaps cannot be corrected and checked in the available time, retain what was established. Identify each unresolved requirement and the additional time, task, provider contribution or decision it would need. Keep the remaining work outside the present allocation unless a change is authorized.

#### HCD.9:4.6 - Decide the Episode Outcome without Overclaiming

Use the outcome supported by the episode.

- **changed action under recorded conditions:** the retry shows the intended correction or discrimination with its actual support;
- **supported action retained:** the criterion and relevant response support keeping the action within the stated conditions; another attempt or verbal explanation addresses a remaining question when needed;
- **unchanged or recurring difficulty:** the same relevant error remains after usable feedback and a valid retry;
- **new or differently located difficulty:** the retry changes the diagnosis or exposes another dependency;
- **safe stop or incomplete episode:** risk, missing access, provider failure, time, or task invalidity prevents a required attempt, use of feedback or retry.

A changed action and an adequately retained action are useful local results. Scope each to the task and help observed. Further claims about cause, independence, transfer or retention require suitable evidence. A difficulty or safe stop can justify changing the selected development method, task, support or practice focus without establishing a general incapacity.

#### HCD.9:4.7 - Return the Practice-Episode Result

Preserve the conditions and observations needed to interpret the episode.

| Result position | Required content |
| --- | --- |
| episode boundary | Holder, target, Method, task, practice focus, conditions, criteria, protected errors, and receiving use |
| first attempt | Learner action and work product, time, uncertainty, and support state before feedback |
| actual help | Sources, tools, AI, peers, teachers, specialists, cues, demonstrations, and when each was received |
| observation | The criterion-bearing action, success, error or uncertainty observed, any plausible causes still unresolved or the cause the evidence establishes, and the aspects of the response that remain sound |
| feedback | Exact content, provider, timing, channel, intended next action, risk boundary, and opportunity to use it |
| response and any retry | The learner’s response and grounds for changing or retaining the action. Include a verbal explanation where it matters, and the conditions, result and support for any required retry or the reason for stopping. |
| disposition | `changed action under recorded conditions`, `supported action retained`, `unchanged difficulty`, `new difficulty`, or `safe stop/incomplete` |
| continuation | The next practice focus, needed task or support change, or reason for stopping. Identify any remaining consequential gap and what would reopen it. Include a stronger evidence question when the use requires the stronger claim. |

Retain enough detail for the next use. One whole task can exercise several methods. Preserve the differences between its first, helped, corrected, transfer or delayed responses where the intended claim depends on them.

#### HCD.9:4.8 - Recognition and Assurance

**Recognition.** Use HCD.9 when a learner is about to practise, or when a completed episode leaves open what they tried, which help or feedback reached them, how they responded and whether another attempt is needed. A completion mark alone leaves those facts open.

**Assurance.** For stronger reliance, establish that the task represents the work and that the criteria are qualified for it. Preserve the first-attempt conditions, help received, usable feedback and the learner’s response. Preserve a safe stopping boundary and any required retry. Qualify the conclusion to the observed conditions. If the issue concerns employment, release, authorization or protected subject criteria, identify the relevant rule or decision holder. Use the applicable evidence method for a transfer or retention claim.

#### HCD.9:4.9 - What Changes in Practice

Identify what the learner tried, what help was received, the criterion addressed by the feedback and why the response should change or remain. Use a comparable retry for the affected requirement after correction, or for a remaining question after retention. Stop when the practice question is answered.

#### HCD.9:4.10 - Coach scientific reasoning during process improvement

Use this application when the learner is practising the Improvement Kata in E.23:4.4.1. Start with the selected process, the intended improvement and available observations. Locate the learner's work in the inquiry. They may be studying current work, forming a target condition or choosing a step toward it. Observe the reasoning the current task requires. It may involve distinguishing facts from explanations, constructing a useful target condition, identifying an obstacle, choosing an informative step, predicting what it will reveal and using its result to revise the next action. A process improvement and a change in the learner’s reasoning each need evidence about their own subject.

**Prepare a task that exposes the reasoning.** Begin with a process the learner can examine and affect safely. Its consequences must be observable soon enough for feedback to be useful. Establish which errors require intervention and what help is available. The learner prepares observations and a proposal for the next step. Use a board, notes, the source’s starter forms or another accessible way to recover the target, actual condition, prediction and result. For a novice, the starter questions can also guide the conversation. Adapt the format as long as those distinctions remain available.

**Examine the learner's reasoning.** Ask the learner to explain the target, current condition and latest step, as far as each has been established. Compare the explanation with the facts and the process-improvement method. The familiar questions help recover the target, establish the present condition, identify an obstacle, select a next step and its expected result, and agree when to examine what happened. For a completed step, compare the earlier prediction with its observed result. Use the questions that reveal the reasoning at issue.

A learner may know where a defect occurs while its cause remains unknown. An old baseline may leave the present condition uncertain. A proposed action may have no apparent bearing on the obstacle. Locate the first unsupported connection in the learner’s explanation. Ask how they reached that inference and allow time for the answer. Give the explanation or demonstration needed for the learner’s next attempt. EXD.5 can help with expressing or constructing the explanation itself.

When the work needs an observation, use a suitable existing result or help the learner identify an attainable observation. Address a mistaken inference from adequate facts. Retain a proposed step whose grounds already fit. If the exercise is to choose a next step, it can finish once the learner identifies a useful safe step, what they expect to learn and when its result can be examined. Early work can consist of understanding the challenge, studying the present process or constructing the target. For a review of a completed step, the observed comparison can answer the practice question.

**Make feedback usable in the next attempt.** Identify what the learner did, why it matters and what to practise next. An instruction to be more specific can leave the missing move obscure. If the recorded times predate a form change, ask the learner to distinguish today’s lookup, typing and correction times before deciding what automation would address. Let the learner formulate the observation and carry it out where the task permits. On return, examine how the proposal uses the evidence. Retain what was already well grounded.

In E.23’s contract case the learner proposes automation before establishing what currently causes delay. On a comparable retry, current observations show that customer clarification has become material and lookup no longer makes a material contribution to the delay. Repeating the lookup remedy misses the obstacle. The learner can identify the information needed, a source and an observation that would justify a change. Interpret that response in light of the help the learner received. Independent or durable capability requires further grounds.

**Develop the coach through observed coaching.** When the coaching itself is the practice target, a second coach observes an interaction or uses an adequate record of it. Examine what the learner said, the gap the coach noticed, the help offered and what the learner did next. Invite the coach’s interpretation and compare it with particular observations. If further practice is needed, select a practicable focus and agree what the second coach will observe. The learner’s process work remains theirs to perform.

A coach who immediately answers the automation question may leave the learner’s inference about delay unexamined. Using the earlier timing claim, the second coach can suggest that the first coach ask the learner how they established the present delay, let the learner finish and help at the missing connection. When the learner already makes that comparison, an interruption can obstruct it. Decide from the interaction whether feedback, rehearsal or another observation would help. Competence in Improvement Kata prepares a coach for the work. Evidence of coaching concerns the interaction itself.

**Change the support as performance changes.** Begin with enough structure and observation for the learner or coach to perform the reasoning. Use observed attempts and the next task to decide which support to retain, change, reduce or restore. HCD.10 addresses that choice across episodes. A harder process may require new subject knowledge even when the reasoning routine is familiar. Schedule coaching so that feedback arrives in time and the process and providers can sustain it. Rother offers practice counts and short daily meetings as guidance. Evidence of skill comes from the person’s work.

When the target is reached or the agreed date arrives, examine what happened in the process and in the learner’s practice. Which inference became better grounded or was already sound? What help did the learner use, and what difficulty remains? If the coach’s contribution is also at issue, assess it from the interaction. The episode can end with an observed correction or reasoned retention under the stated help. HCD.11–HCD.13 address a remaining question about performance, transfer or retention.

### HCD.9:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.9:5.1 - Redirect a Highest-NPV Answer to the Tested Configuration

In the release case the learner selects external module B because its stipulated NPV is highest. Ordinary references and calculation tools are permitted. The financial comparison is useful, but the learner relies on a vendor report without checking which firmware it covers.

The teacher asks, “Which configuration does the report support?” The learner finds FW7 in the report and FW8 in the release requirement. They retain the conditional financial comparison, request compatible evidence from the supplier and withhold reliance on module B for this release until suitable evidence for the required configuration supports its use. Evidence covering another candidate would have to fit that candidate’s own configuration. The learner has corrected the grounds of the original answer.

On the retry a compatible HW3/FW8/SCHED2 report is available. Three homogeneous batches of ten changes in total require 23 test hours. A 24-hour allowance covers them, while demand of twelve leaves a queue. With only 22 hours, a promise of ten changes fails the time condition. Observe whether the learner changes the answer with the evidence and available time, including what help they use. This retry concerns the tested conditions.

#### HCD.9:5.2 - Turn a Pump Claim into a Discriminating Observation

Use the public pump task in HCD.6:5.1, including its 20 kW/100 m³/h baseline, measurement uncertainty, comparison model and protected observation time. The learner's attempt uses 22.3 kW and 99.5 m³/h and concludes that increased energy per volume proves higher resistance. The calculation and supplied uncertainty bounds support the increase and weaken the measurement-error explanation; resistance and regulation efficiency remain rivals.

The practitioner has a qualified worked comparison and does not yet know whether this learner can use it. After preserving the first answer, give the learner the comparison. Ask where the conclusion exceeds the evidence and what action the comparison supports. If the learner explains the rival causes and chooses an observation, a later episode can start with the learner’s own answer before providing the comparison. The present attempt shows what the learner did with that help. Detection of the original error before help remains a separate question.

If the learner repeats “we need pressure,” ask how each possible pressure result affects the two explanations under the supplied model. A value near 448 kPa supports increased resistance under the stated conditions. A value near 400 kPa redirects attention toward regulation efficiency. These conditional predictions leave the actual pressure and any unique cause open. If the learner still cannot use the distinction, HCD.6.1 can help design that practice. Use a suitable existing explanation or obtain the help still needed through HCD.7 before expecting an unaided retry when the practice question calls for one.

The learner preserves the calculation, qualifies the causal claim and explains how the possible results of a comparable pressure observation would affect the next decision. They request that observation within the remaining one and a half specialist-hours supplied by HCD.6:5.1. The learning arrangement separately needs time for explanation, individual feedback and any retry. The corrected learner contribution is the conditional explanation and choice of observation.

A later case changes the uncertainty or removes access to comparable pressure data. The learner weighs any attainable observation against its preparation, specialist time, comparison and displaced work. If none contributes enough, the learner can return the supported energy-per-volume change and the two qualified explanations to the responsible practitioner. The cause remains unresolved and a resistance-specific remedy lacks grounds. This can be a successful retry under the stated criteria.

If the changed conditions make the pressure observation both worthwhile and obtainable within the window, select it and explain how the possible values would affect the response. The observation result remains unknown until measured. In both cases the energy calculation leaves the cause open. Any operating protection depends on its own conditions and authority.

#### HCD.9:5.3 - Fit a Targeted Retry into Three Hours

The programme's retry slot allocates 135 minutes to the learner's correction and short changed case, 15 minutes to an individual teacher check, and 30 minutes to recording the result: three hours in total. The teacher chooses a case small enough for the affected requirement to be checked in that interval.

Keep requirements already demonstrated unless the new response contradicts them. If several independent gaps cannot be corrected and checked in the slot, record those still open. Further work requires agreement about time or a narrower output. The 340-hour programme and any group-level result leave that individual limit in place.

#### HCD.9:5.4 - Preserve the First Attempt and Attribute Demonstration and AI Help

A teacher may demonstrate one move on an anchor case before giving the learner a distinct variant. Give the variant’s conditions first and keep its answer and key with the teacher. If difficulty prompts a detailed cue or demonstration, identify the help when reporting the learner’s correction.

AI can search, calculate, draft or critique within the permitted use. Record the learner’s question before AI use, what the tool supplied, the decisive source and calculation checks, and how the learner explained and used the output. Attribute the generated revision to the tool. The learner’s checking and use of it can establish their own supported correction. HCD.10 can help select a later task with changed support, and HCD.11–HCD.13 govern the resulting inference.

#### HCD.9:5.5 - Retain a Sound Choice after Feedback

In a constructed practice case, an import specialist must decide whether a successful result in format V1 justifies using the same procedure for V2. The supplied criterion requires a check compatible with the receiving format. Before help, the specialist notices that the automated check supports V1 only and returns the V2 validation question to its owner. The feedback confirms the format mismatch and asks what makes the return warranted. The specialist points to the check's declared scope and retains the decision.

If the practice question was whether the specialist noticed the mismatch and could return it to the appropriate source, the first attempt and explanation suffice. Record that the supported action was retained. If the purpose includes recognising when to proceed, the learner still needs a comparable case with a V2-compatible check, time and qualified feedback. The first refusal establishes only the discrimination shown.

### HCD.9:6 - Bias-Annotation

Lenses: **Gov**, **Arch**, **Onto/Epist**, **Prag**, **Did**. Examine one focused practice episode and how its feedback bears on the learner’s action.

| Recurring bias | Likely drift | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| hours-dose bias | Logged time is treated as the mechanism or proof of improvement. | Identify the task, what the learner did, the help and feedback received, and any correction or retry. |
| corrected-product bias | The final answer overwrites the first attempt and received help. | Preserve the first response, what the provider contributed, what the learner did with it and any subsequent retry. |
| answer-substitution bias | Teacher, peer, or AI output becomes the learner's performance. | Require a learner action after the contribution and retain attribution. |
| score-only bias | A mark identifies a threshold while the learner still needs to know what to do. | Identify the criterion, what the learner did well, any error and the next action or grounds for retaining the current one. |
| feedback-immediacy bias | One timing rule is applied regardless of risk and purpose. | Choose timing from safety, consequence, first-attempt value, and error rehearsal. |
| exact-repeat bias | Memorizing the corrected answer is mistaken for rule use. | Change a decision-bearing condition when discrimination or adaptation matters. |
| total-retest bias | One defect causes every supported requirement to be tested again. | Retry the affected requirement. Reopen another when new evidence calls its result into question or a change makes it relevant again. |
| practice-effect bias | A changed attempt is used as proof of capability, transfer, retention or programme effect. | Report what the episode supports. Use the applicable assessment or evaluation method if the task needs a stronger inference. |

### HCD.9:7 - Conformance Checklist

- [ ] Identify the learner, later work, selected method, representative task, practice focus, criteria and intended use of the result.
- [ ] Establish that the needed providers, access and support are available in time for the learner to use feedback and make any required retry. Identify when to stop safely or report an unavailable condition.
- [ ] The first attempt is preserved before answer-bearing help when independent action is part of the purpose.
- [ ] Intended, permitted, available, and received help remain distinct.
- [ ] Identify the observed action addressed by the feedback and the evidence for changing or retaining it.
- [ ] Feedback identifies the relevant attempt, criterion, useful part, any error or uncertainty, and the next learner action or grounds for retention.
- [ ] Choose feedback timing from the purpose, risk, consequence of delay and value of observing the first response.
- [ ] Identify what the learner did and what the provider supplied. If the learner retained a sound action, check the evidence the target calls for. Ask for a verbal justification when explaining the grounds is part of the target or is needed to settle the remaining question.
- [ ] After a correction, use a comparable retry to check the affected requirement. Change a relevant condition when the target includes discrimination or adaptation. A sound action already established for the stated question can end the episode.
- [ ] Previously supported requirements are preserved unless the new response contradicts them or makes them material again.
- [ ] Identify any independent requirement that remains open, what can continue safely and what would allow further practice if it is needed.
- [ ] Report the performance and support observed under the episode conditions. For a causal, capability, transfer or retention claim, establish the additional grounds that claim needs.

### HCD.9:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “Practise for ten more hours” | Duration leaves the action, difficulty and feedback unspecified. | Select one practice focus and establish what the learner does with the feedback. |
| “Feedback was provided” | Its content, recipient, timing and opportunity for use remain unknown. | Identify what reached the learner, how it bore on the criterion and what the learner did with it. |
| “Here is the correct answer” | Provider output can replace the learner action. | Have the learner use the information in the relevant action; record the help and obtain a learner-authored correction when one is needed. |
| “The corrected file proves mastery” | The first attempt and support have disappeared. | Recover the attempt, the help received, the learner’s response and any retry from the available evidence. |
| “Repeat the same question” | Answer memory can mimic the intended discrimination. | Change the condition that should change the warranted move. |
| “Retake the whole module” | Already supported requirements and the exact gap are lost. | Retry the affected requirement and preserve compatible success. |
| “Improvement after feedback proves causality or durable capability” | Temporal order does not establish either conclusion. | Report changed performance under the recorded conditions. Seek stronger evidence only when the receiving use needs the stronger claim. |
| “Everyone passed overall” | A critical or individual unresolved gap is hidden by aggregation. | Keep holder-level requirements, safe stops, and continuations visible. |

### HCD.9:9 - Consequences

The learner can use feedback to change or retain a particular action. The practitioner can explain what the learner did before and after help, which requirements the work supports and which errors remain. If another episode is needed, those observations help choose its focus.

Observing and documenting the episode takes time from the learner and the provider. An episode needs observable criteria, timely feedback, an opportunity to use it and time for any required retry. Evidence about the help received may limit what an improved product establishes about the learner. Some difficulties exceed the planned slot.

### HCD.9:10 - Rationale

For feedback to contribute to learning, it must reach the learner in a form and at a time they can use. Examine what they did with it. The first attempt provides a basis for selecting help and interpreting their later response.
