| Visibility and exploration | Seeing another solution can support learning while displacing one's own useful search or hiding the original judgement. |
| Material continuity and burden | Preserving work across activities can enable comparison while producing reading and integration costs. |
| Shared performance and evidence | The task can provide useful observations without establishing individual transfer or a causal learning effect. |

### HCD.22:4 - Solution

#### HCD.22:4.1 - Keep the whole work question and choose the dependence

Start from the whole work question, its purpose and recipient. Establish the subject criteria, meaningful conditions, critical errors and permitted help using the qualified task or HCD.6 where these inputs are missing. Retain the purpose when dividing the work.

Choose the dependence that serves the intended operation:

| Dependence | Useful construction | Characteristic failure and repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Different evidence or information | Participants interpret distinct relevant observations and make them usable for a joint inference. | A participant reads a fragment verbatim without interpreting it, or a missing fragment blocks the comparison. Have its holder explain what the observation implies for the common inference. Restore missing qualified content if feasible, or state which inference remains blocked. |
| Different interpretations or grounds | Participants compare defensible rival models, objections or solutions against common conditions. | A vote replaces examination. Require the condition and evidence that support or defeat each option. |
| Complementary work parts | Several contributions must be integrated into a result whose interfaces matter. | Each learns only their assigned fragment although everyone needs the whole. Add the required cross-part explanation or later task, or narrow the target explicitly. |
| Shared equipment or action | Participants perform useful observer and operator actions around a limited resource. | Observation is empty or substitutes for required manipulation. Specify the observer's judgement and provide the necessary personal turns. |
| Explanation to a recipient | A learner makes a relation intelligible enough for someone else to use and responds to questions about it. | Fluent speech is accepted without evidence of use. Where use is the criterion, have the recipient apply or distinguish the relation and return any remaining difficulty to the explainer. An observed adequate application can answer the question. |

Use each dependency for the contribution it adds and allow for its cost. Added secrecy, delay or scarce access can prevent learning. If individual work supports the required actions better, retain that option in the arrangement comparison.

Require a common answer when the purpose depends on it. Participants can profitably contrast their own models and revise them without creating a separate team report. Where a common result matters, define how it must use the constituent contributions.

#### HCD.22:4.2 - Make each required action consequential

For each target, identify what the learner must do and how the task will use or reveal their contribution. A diagnostic learner might propose rival causes, interpret a measurement, challenge an assumption or choose a discriminating observation. If the target requires another participant to use that contribution, design the comparison or response that makes this use possible.

Allocate actions across preparation, interaction and later attempts. Give a new analyst an opportunity to do the analysis; to establish that the action rotated, check who performed it. A recorder can learn to reconcile inconsistent claims or preserve the conditions of a conclusion. Copying notes does not establish model selection.

Choose a personal first attempt when the learner has enough preparation and the initial judgement matters for diagnosis, comparison or protection from premature copying. Preserve it before feedback so a later correction can be interpreted. When the learner first needs a demonstration, supply it. For a subsequent test of independent choice, select a task that leaves the decisive choice to the learner. For supported work, preserve the help the target permits.

At shared equipment, a non-operator can predict, identify a mismatch, choose a pause or measurement, and explain a consequence. Give each learner who must develop control an attainable personal turn. Rotate operators where that supplies the required turns. Determine how the result is observed without making unnecessary written reporting displace the physical or interpersonal work.

For a target of review or explanation, an AI or peer contribution can supply a useful comparison or help. Identify what the learner is to judge, change or explain. Use evidence of that action when making a personal performance claim.

##### HCD.22:4.2.1 - Learn joint work while preserving different roles

Separate learning **through** a group from learning **to work together**. A discussion can improve each engineer's model selection even if they later work separately. A team may instead need to coordinate different qualified contributions in a design review, operation or exception response. In the latter case, the connection between actions is part of the learning target.

For learning to work together, identify the episode, required contributions and how the people in each role use them. Include an exception when handling it matters. Establish what can signal a need for clarification or help and how a missing or incompatible result can be recovered. Select a connection the team needs to learn or sustain. For example, a calculation can depend on clarification of a requirement, a judgement on a revised configuration, or a decision on a timely reply.

For a practice episode, use information and timing representative of the receiving task. Have participants supply, use or return a contribution and examine the joint action. For a question about completed work, use a suitable existing episode. A workflow description can prepare a practice attempt. Reduce unrelated difficulty or supply a qualified specialist result when this preserves the coordination being learned. Retain any uncertainty or response window that makes the connection necessary.

Teach enough about another role to anticipate its need and interpret its response. A perspective-taking exercise or bounded role exchange can expose that need; it does not authorize professional substitution or require everyone to master every role. Keep the intended specialization when it serves the work. Provide personal execution when the target requires it and use role rotation when it helps provide that opportunity.

Review the episode under the roles, information and help present. If another occasion is needed and feasible, select an adjustment when one would improve the connection, such as a clearer request, an escalation cue or a checked handover. Evidence about personal action and team coordination answers different questions. If responsibilities, access, workflow or the team’s method need to change, act within the applicable authority or seek a decision from its holder. Use OCE for an organization question.

#### HCD.22:4.3 - Choose visibility and personal memory separately

Decide what participants can see at each useful point: raw observations, reasons, candidate answers, a common model or feedback. Explain what that access enables. A hidden answer can preserve an initial judgement; a shared diagram can make a relation available for simultaneous examination. Choose the timing that preserves the intended action.

Decide separately whether personal work is retained and how it can be reused. A saved initial answer helps identify revision but may also anchor later search. If a new attempt is meant to expose a fresh model choice, state which previous material remains a legitimate reference. If the decisive choice was shown, interpret the later response under that assistance.

Bernstein, Shore and Lazer's experiment distinguishes exposure to others' solutions from storage of one's own best solution. Designers can therefore vary access to other solutions separately from access to a learner’s own saved solution. The experiment concerns triads solving a travelling-salesperson problem and different measures of solution quality; it does not prescribe a visibility schedule for this diagnostic lesson or demonstrate later personal transfer.

After interaction, make needed qualified content accessible to everyone who must use it. Temporary distribution can prompt exchange; permanently withholding another participant's portion can prevent the later whole-task performance.

#### HCD.22:4.4 - Connect activities through usable material

For each consequential transition, identify what is available or must be produced, any transformation it needs, and how the next participant can use it. In a design, establish what would make the transfer feasible. For a claim of completed transfer, use evidence from the actual contributions and recipients.

For example, “annotate before the meeting” leaves the central connection unspecified. A useful annotation identifies the claim, its relevant evidence, the proposed interpretation and any open question. Before the meeting, the assigned recipient can access the annotations and select materially different interpretations where they exist. Participants compare their grounds and pass on the supported result or the disagreement that remains.

A shared board must preserve source and condition where their removal changes the inference. Compressing “consistent with resistance if flow and efficiency are unchanged” to “resistance” destroys the basis of the comparison. A summary may simplify presentation while preserving that condition.

For a missing, late, inaccessible or incorrect contribution, identify a qualified substitute, reassignment, explanation or delay that keeps the task feasible. If none is available, report the limit. A supplied answer may restore the group’s work. If a learner missed an intended action, keep that fact in the account of the episode. If another opportunity is still needed, arrange it when feasible or report what remains unavailable.

Check usability when work passes to another medium, group or time and the change could affect the recipient’s next action. Private notes may not be shareable, a screenshot may be unreadable or a report may omit the disputed observation. For a completed transfer, establish what reached the recipient and whether it was usable. For a claim that they used it, establish what they did.

#### HCD.22:4.5 - Select a coherent variant and adapt its working mechanism

Two established designs illustrate different dependencies.

**Team-Based Learning.** The [official account](https://www.teambasedlearning.org/learn-tbl) connects preparation, individual readiness work, a team response to the same questions, immediate feedback, appeals and instructor clarification with application to a significant common problem requiring a specific choice and simultaneous reporting. Its purpose is not simply sitting in teams. If borrowing only the comparison of individual and team reasons, describe that adaptation and supply its needed preparation and feedback; do not imply implementation of the whole design. Fixed membership and assessment practices in the source are properties of that design, not rules for all HCD tasks.

**Jigsaw.** The [official account](https://www.jigsaw.org/overview/) distributes parts, uses expert-group preparation and rehearsal, then returns participants to teach their home groups, with individual assessment. The expert's contribution is therefore something others must be able to learn and use. In an adaptation, prepare a way to restore an absent or mistaken part and test the recipient's use. Simply dividing a report into sections omits that teaching dependence. The source's illustrative group size is not a size criterion for another task.

For either variant, state what has changed, why the learning mechanism remains plausible, and what evidence could qualify its use in the new setting. Avoid combining labels whose timing, preparation or feedback assumptions conflict. Another construction, including active shared-equipment work, can be more suitable.

#### HCD.22:4.6 - Make disagreement and feedback lead to another action

Where disagreement matters, specify how participants can support a claim, request clarification, test a rival and respond. A useful challenge names evidence or a condition that would defeat the inference. A response can justify keeping, qualifying or revising the conclusion. Obtain a needed observation when it is available and the task calls for it, or identify what remains unresolved.

Use a qualified subject check for errors the participants cannot settle. A peer may expose a conflict and a facilitator may organize turns while the domain judgement still needs a qualified source. Use an existing answer when it covers the question. Use HCD.7 to arrange needed support and HCD.8 to compare obtaining or developing a missing contribution, or identify what remains unavailable.

Give the recipient a chance to use feedback. A score can flag trouble while leaving its cause unclear. Feedback can point to an unsupported inference, supply a contrast or elicit a justified next observation. The learner may correct an error or explain why a sound first answer should stand. Preserve what the first attempt showed and what help was then used. Select another attempt when it could answer a remaining question.

Protect the intended learning work when AI or a strong peer can complete the product faster. They can model, challenge or check, but give the learner an opportunity to perform the operation being developed and distinguish it from the supplied part. If the encompassing purpose changes to rapid delivery of a work product, that division of labour can legitimately change; return the changed purpose rather than preserving unnecessary teaching activity.

HCD.23 develops mutual explanation and the personal return; HCD.24 develops peer judgement and the author's use of feedback; HCD.25 develops comparison across projects with a breaking condition. Select the contribution the task needs. When participants must recover their shared course of action, HCD.26 supplies observation, process help and inspection of uptake. HCD.27 develops the preparation, material-transfer and re-entry windows connecting separate episodes.

#### HCD.22:4.7 - Observe the relevant result and return the next need

Select a personal return that exposes the target under appropriate conditions: a revised explanation, an individual decision on changed data, a physical performance, or a contribution in another integrated task. Use the performed work directly when it supplies the needed observation.

A correction with feedback, an uncued choice on a new case and delayed performance support different interpretations. Use HCD.11–HCD.13 for the corresponding human-evidence question. The quality of the common answer, participant activity and material contribution remain separately reportable.

Locate a failure at the connection it affects. An unused annotation may indicate a transfer or task problem. A correct answer from one participant leaves the others’ work open. An unfamiliar term can point to preparation or material repair, and a late answer can reveal a supply problem. Use HCD.20 when changed size, access or burden affects the arrangement comparison, and HCD.28 for the affected dependencies of the whole product.

### HCD.22:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.22:5.1 - A shared diagnosis with individual model selection

The constructed task for HCD.28’s future diagnosticians uses supplied data and a qualified subject criterion. Testing an operating pump would require separate permission and conditions.

The baseline is 100 m³/h, 400 kPa and 20 kW. A later observation reports the same flow and 22.4 kW, with pressure still unknown. The group must recommend a warranted next observation and a bounded diagnostic conclusion. Each participant must learn to distinguish a ratio change from evidence selecting its cause.

After a worked contrast, each records an initial explanation from the common data. The record shows whether “12% more energy per volume” has already become “12% more resistance” without the needed assumptions. References and arithmetic tools remain available; an answer naming the preferred model is withheld during this particular first choice.

For four participants, prepare four accessible contributions:

| Contribution | What its holder must do | Use in the common result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Measurement evidence | Interpret a repeat power reading of 22.3 ± 0.2 kW and flow of 99.5 ± 1 m³/h against the baseline. | Test whether the stated measurement uncertainty could remove the ratio increase. |
| Resistance model | Explain what pressure change would be expected if flow and efficiency were unchanged. | Supply the pressure predicted under the stated conditions. |
| Rival model | Explain how changed efficiency or regulation can produce a different relation and what remains unknown. | Prevent a resistance explanation from being accepted merely because it is familiar. |
| Observation budget and access | Compare the obtainable observations and their effort under the remaining allowance. | Select an informative observation available within the allowance. |

The group has four specialist-hours for measurements in this constructed setting. The repeated power and flow work costs one and one-and-a-half hours respectively, leaving one-and-a-half hours for the available pressure observation. Each holder explains their contribution and challenges or answers a consequential question about another contribution. The two three-minute contributions per person and six minutes of reconciliation use thirty minutes. HCD.20:5.1 adds a separate six-minute qualified-help visit after all four initial explanations and before the second personal round. Its staggered starts and named mentor assignments therefore require thirty-six active minutes per group; help does not occupy the time already promised for personal reasoning.

The smallest ratio allowed by the stated readings, 22.1/100.5, exceeds the baseline 20/100. The stated uncertainty does not erase the increase or determine its cause. At unchanged flow and efficiency the resistance model predicts 448 kPa. A sufficiently accurate pressure observation fits the remaining allowance and can test that prediction. A compatible reading would still leave more than one explanation open.

Provide the selected observation after the participants justify its use. In one branch it is compatible with 448 kPa; the resistance account remains a conditional candidate, not a unique proven cause. In another it is compatible with the 400 kPa baseline; the simple unchanged-efficiency resistance explanation no longer accounts for the power change. In that branch, identify the remaining efficiency, regulation or measurement question for the engineer.

The group result retains the observations, model conditions, chosen test and remaining uncertainty. It identifies which earlier inference the new evidence supports, qualifies or changes, and why. A facilitator can accept that bounded result when the observations leave the cause open.

Then each participant receives a changed case, with the same subject comparison available as a reference but no peer, mentor or AI supplying the model choice. The ten-minute personal attempt asks what the observations support and what the receiving engineer should do next. Interpret the group practice, the person’s first response and any subsequent correction under the conditions of each.

**Personal case: the pressure result is already available.** Reuse HCD.6's baseline of 100 m³/h, 400 kPa and 20 kW. The supplied independent results are 22.3 ± 0.2 kW, 99.5 ± 1 m³/h and 400 ± 4 kPa, compatible with the pressure baseline. The four specialist-hours have been used on those three observations. No further worthwhile observation is obtainable in the present window, and the day-long shutdown is outside the allowed arrangement. The receiving engineer needs the supported diagnostic result within the present window.

The learner may use the quantity definitions, arithmetic tools and HCD.6's conditional subject comparison. They must interpret the existing pressure result, retain the live explanation or uncertainty, and justify their next step or the decision to end this inquiry within its stated limits. Keep the worked responses below with the provider during this attempt; showing them would change the help supplied.

A plausible wrong response is: “The indicator rose by about 12%, so the increased resistance should be corrected.” The ratio increase survives the stated power/flow uncertainty, but the unchanged-efficiency resistance account predicted a pressure near 448 kPa. The supplied pressure does not support that prediction. A second pressure request would also spend effort obtaining a result already available.

A warranted personal return distinguishes the indicator change from its cause. The increase remains, the simple resistance account under its stated assumptions is unsupported, and regulation, efficiency or measurement explanations outside the stated uncertainty remain open. Give the engineer the observations, rejected conditional inference and remaining uncertainty. No resistance-specific remedy follows. The inquiry can end here because no further worthwhile observation is obtainable.

If the first response still infers resistance from the ratio, feedback points to the pressure condition and asks the learner to rewrite the diagnostic return. The learner reads the feedback and revises within HCD.28's fifteen-minute feedback-and-correction period. That corrected return demonstrates work with this assistance; it does not replace the preserved first response or establish unassisted transfer. For a later claim about transfer or retention, use evidence that represents its required conditions under HCD.11–HCD.13.

#### HCD.22:5.2 - Recover a missing contribution without pretending learning occurred

Suppose the measurement-evidence participant is absent. A prepared qualified card can restore those data and their interpretation to the group. Assign a present participant to explain how the uncertainty changes the inference, adjusting the time construction if needed. The group can proceed if the restored contribution is usable.

The absent participant did not explain the measurement or select the model in this episode. Offer a viable individual or later shared task when their missed opportunity still needs to be supplied. If no such route is available, report the gap. A signed group report may establish the group’s result.

Suppose instead the card is present but compresses the conclusion to “measurement is not the cause.” Repair its claim: the stated uncertainty does not explain away this ratio increase; that does not eliminate every possible measurement fault. The error belongs to the supplied material and its dependent conclusion. It is not evidence that learners need more motivation.

#### HCD.22:5.3 - Shared equipment and an explanation without a report

In a safe instrument-training task, one participant operates while others predict, identify a mismatch or select a measurement. The operator uses that contribution and explains the response; roles then change so that required control actions are personally performed. No private first answer is necessary before a novice has seen how to use the instrument. A later claim of independent interpretation needs an attempt in which the learner makes the decisive choice.

A different task asks one participant to explain why two visually similar technical passages imply different actions. The recipient applies each passage to a small case, exposes an ambiguity and requests a repair. The explainer revises the account and the recipient retries. The learning interaction can be complete without a common written report. The result is the explained distinction and its observed use, with any help and remaining difficulty preserved.

### HCD.22:6 - Bias-Annotation

| Likely drift | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| Fluent-speaker bias | Inspect the grounds and the recipient’s use when judging the explanation. Confidence or speaking time can coexist with an unusable account. |
| Consensus bias | Preserve a warranted disagreement or unknown instead of rewarding convergence. |
| Role-label bias | Name and observe the operation performed in the role. |
| Visibility optimism | Choose what access enables and what initial reasoning it would conceal. |
| Fragment-completion bias | Return each learned part to the whole task and the contribution promised for each learner. |
| Submission-as-transfer bias | Inspect whether the recipient can use the submitted material. |

### HCD.22:7 - Conformance Checklist

A usable task description lets the participants and provider identify:

- the whole task, qualified criteria, target personal actions and any common result;
- the selected dependence and the contribution it makes to learning;
- adequate preparation, the help required, what can be supplied under the proposed conditions, and how to handle unresolved subject questions;
- action allocation, visibility and personal-work retention appropriate to that purpose;
- usable transfers between activities and a feasible recovery or explicit limit for missing or wrong content;
- feedback that lets the learner correct an error or justify keeping a sound answer, and any personal return needed for the learning purpose;
- what each available observation establishes and what it leaves open.

A design specifies the intended actions and observations. It can support a feasibility finding to the extent that its conditions are established. To report performance, establish which actions, help and results occurred. For personal capability, use the corresponding conditions in HCD.11–HCD.13. A causal claim about learning requires an appropriate research basis.

### HCD.22:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Anti-pattern | Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One solver, many names | The task permits bypassing the intended personal work. | Design a use for each necessary operation and an opportunity to observe it. For a claim about performance, establish what each participant did, using existing observations where sufficient. |
| Artificial dependence | Secrecy or scarce access obstructs work without adding learning. | Retain only the dependence that serves the selected contribution. |
| Test before needed preparation | A private test precedes teaching even when the method is unavailable. | Supply modelling or preparation, then select an interpretable attempt. |
| Discussion by vote | Popularity replaces a subject criterion. | Compare grounds, discriminating conditions and a qualified return. |
| Scheduled but unconnected | The next participant cannot use the earlier result, or the evidence of delivery is missing. | In a design, specify how the recipient can obtain and use it. For a claim of completed transfer, establish what reached the recipient and in what usable form. |
| Unrecoverable expert | A needed contribution is missing or incorrect. | Use a qualified substitute when available or identify what the group cannot yet do. Arrange any missed personal learning opportunity separately when feasible, or report the remaining gap. |
| Universal final report | Documentation displaces a bodily, explanatory or interpersonal target. | Preserve only the common result needed for the work and inference. |

### HCD.22:9 - Consequences

The designer can explain why participants need one another, what each must do and what the interaction could contribute to a subsequent attempt. Recovery can preserve a group task without misreporting an absent participant's learning. Different tasks can use different visibility, products and roles.

Allow for the cost of preparing the contributions, feedback, material transfers and recovery the selected task requires. More detailed coordination can itself obstruct a simple task; remove it when the same learning contribution is available with less work. Reopen the design when a participant can bypass the target operation, a transfer fails, help changes or the common result no longer serves the learning purpose.

### HCD.22:10 - Architectural Rationale

A shared task is a composition of learning actions, subject criteria and material dependencies. The common product and each learner's contribution can change independently. Specify how the shared task uses each necessary personal action and what each result can establish.

A generic group exercise leaves these connections implicit. A fixed private–group–private sequence is easier to repeat and fits tasks that need a prior judgement, interaction and a later personal response. The selected method derives the dependence and evidence from the purpose, permits modelling and active observation, and retains individual work wherever the promised contribution requires it.

### HCD.22:11 - SoTA-Echoing

The official [TBL](https://www.teambasedlearning.org/learn-tbl) and [Jigsaw](https://www.jigsaw.org/overview/) accounts supply the distinct constructions summarized in §4.5. Their combination or adaptation here does not transfer an effectiveness claim.

[Bernstein, Shore and Lazer, 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6126746/) supplies the bounded visibility/storage distinction in §4.3. Mean and best group solution are different outcomes; neither is a measure of every learner's retained capability.

The [FROG project](https://wonderlab.gse.upenn.edu/projects/frog.html) describes connecting activity outputs across individual asynchronous annotation and synchronous group work. HCD.22 adapts that orchestration idea by making the usable result, recipient and recovery explicit; it makes no causal-effect claim from the project description.

The active-observation possibility is grounded in the [Noerholk et al. study](https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14791) qualified in HCD.20. The diagnostic cards, missing-contribution repair and different explanation task are authored applications. Their feasibility and learning effects remain questions for the corresponding use.

For joint-work learning, the [National Academies' 2025 Team Science account, pp. 59–61](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/29043/chapter/5) connects common working language, cross-training and agreements about roles with the expertise and strategy a team needs. Section 4.2.1 adapts those contributions into practice of a request, usable contribution, recipient response and repair. A common vocabulary or charter can prepare that work; it does not perform the connection.

The historical [ICAP implementation study by Chi and colleagues (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.12626) found that forming groups did not ensure the intended joint construction and that giving test answers could turn an inferential task into recall. This supports §4.2’s check of how another action uses the contribution. The implementation findings concern the activities studied. A ranking across other interactive, constructive, active or passive tasks would need evidence for that comparison.

### HCD.22:12 - Relations

- Start from the learning purpose in HCD.5 or the assignment, qualified whole-task criteria from HCD.6 or the relevant domain, and the arrangement constraints from HCD.20 or other suitable inputs.
- **Uses:** HCD.6.1 for a needed discernment; HCD.7 and HCD.8 for qualified support; HCD.9 for attempts, feedback and correction; HCD.23–HCD.25 for the needed explanation, review or project comparison; HCD.26 and HCD.27 for regulation and compatible continuation.
- Return the task design, a qualified finding about an existing task or the condition that limits it. Where needed, the task can supply executable interaction and observation opportunities to HCD.9, HCD.10 or an evidence question in HCD.11–HCD.13. Use observed work for a claim about what happened.
- Use HCD.19 for a material defect, HCD.20 for a changed arrangement and HCD.28 for dependencies in the whole learning product. For a missing subject judgement, use a qualified source or identify what remains open.
- **Keeps distinct:** useful participant activity, common work-product quality, personal capability, team capability and causal learning effect.

### HCD.22:End

## HCD.23 - Learn through Explanation and Comparison of Solutions

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner mutual-explanation pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.23:0 - Use This When

Use this method when explaining or comparing answers or their grounds can develop reasoning the learners will need. People may agree on a result for different reasons or disagree because one noticed a condition another missed. The task may be to design an exchange, support it or establish what an earlier exchange showed.

In learning through explanation and comparison, participants reconstruct and use the reasoning the task requires and challenge a step when its grounds need examination. A joint product may also be needed. A design can specify how the exchange gives each learner that opportunity. For completed work, return the explained comparison, evidence of a learner’s application under the help used, or the limit of what the exchange establishes.

Begin with the task and criteria that distinguish warranted answers. Where learners need preparation, use a demonstration, an accessible contrast or other suitable instruction. HCD.6.1 can help with a missing distinction. A suitable expert answer can finish a request solely for that answer. If the assignment also calls for learning, use it as appropriate support and preserve the personal operation.

#### HCD.23:0.1 - Working Terms

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| ground | An observation, condition, rule or argument that warrants a step under the subject criterion. |
| explanation | An account connecting the relevant inputs, rule or choice and consequence. It makes the grounds of the answer available for examination. |
| reconstruction | A recipient’s own use of another account’s reasoning to explain or perform the relevant step. |
| personal return | The participant’s own subsequent explanation or action, interpreted in light of the help they received. Distinguish what they used from what was merely available when that affects the claim. |

### HCD.23:1 - Problem Frame

An instructor asks pairs to compare answers. One confident participant states the answer and the other agrees. The second answer sheet is now correct, but the reasoning operation may still be absent. Conversely, two incorrect starting answers can contain grounds that help participants identify a neglected condition, provided the criterion and needed support are accessible.

Design the exchange around a connection worth explaining, a way to question it, a subject criterion and a chance for the learner to use it. Choose a starting point suited to the participants. Their own initial answers can reveal their reasoning. A novice may need a worked example first.

### HCD.23:2 - Problem

How can an exchange of explanations change what each participant can understand and do, while distinguishing that contribution from adopting another person's answer?

### HCD.23:3 - Forces

- Visible differences stimulate questions, while early exposure can erase an informative first judgement.
- Explaining can expose a missing connection, while fluent speech can conceal an invalid one.
- Reciprocal turns broaden participation, while symmetrical speaking time is insufficient evidence of useful reasoning.
- A joint answer coordinates work, while the target may require each person's later selection.
- Help can make a difficult connection learnable, while it changes what the resulting attempt establishes.

### HCD.23:4 - Solution

#### HCD.23:4.1 - Give the exchange a reasoning object

Select a step that matters to the task or the grounds for its answer, such as choosing a model, applying a condition, interpreting an observation or reconciling two results. Make the task, permitted resources and subject criterion accessible. Use HCD.22 to design or assess a needed dependence between contributions. Participants can also examine the same complete material.

Use existing starting responses if they fit the question or obtain them when needed. A short answer with one ground can reveal reasoning a confidence rating leaves open. Preserve the first response when a later comparison depends on it. If a learner needs preparation, show worked attempts or a demonstration and ask them to reconstruct the relevant step. Interpret the result under that assistance.

Decide when others’ answers become visible and whether the learner can use their own previous work. Private preparation can preserve an independently made judgement. Participants may instead need immediate shared access to an event. Retain a previous response when revision or reflection depends on it. A change of visibility or access to earlier work need not change membership.

#### HCD.23:4.2 - Explain a connection and have another person use it

For a new exchange, have the explainer connect the decisive input to the conclusion or action. For a completed one, examine the available explanation and the recipient’s response. Establish which condition applies, why the rule fits and what follows. The recipient can show the step they accept or cannot reconstruct by explaining it, applying it to a variation or identifying evidence that would defeat it. Direct a request for clarification to the unclear step.

Reverse the contribution where both people need practice. One participant may explain the model choice and another challenge the measurement basis, then each handles the other's kind of question in a subsequent attempt. If the task requires active observation, a learner can predict, point to a discrepancy and ask for a pause while another operates the equipment. Choose the turns that give each learner their required action.

Compare the grounds. Establish whether the explanations concern the same observations, conditions and task. When the inputs differ, compare them under a common condition where that serves the question or state how the difference limits comparison. Use a qualified criterion or source for a disputed subject rule. If the source does not resolve it, report the supported part and the remaining question.

#### HCD.23:4.3 - Reconcile without erasing the alternatives

Compare the accounts with the criterion and decisive conditions. Retain sound reasoning and identify any unsupported step. When the work calls for correction and its grounds are available, correct it. State the condition under which the resulting judgement would change when that matters. A comparison can end with justified retention, a bounded choice or a question for a qualified specialist. Prepare a group report when the task needs one.

When arranging practice in the recipient’s own use, have someone other than the original explainer perform or explain the connection. After hearing why batch overhead matters, a listener might calculate a new limit and explain which actions it permits. For a historical claim, use evidence of the particular contribution being reported. If the needed evidence is missing, state the limit. Provide targeted help when the task calls for teaching.

If participants converge on an incorrect account, examine the criterion, shared material and assistance alongside their work. Preserve the original responses needed to understand how the account arose, including any supported first answer abandoned during the exchange. Use a qualified correction or identify what remains disputed. If teaching continues, give participants a feasible occasion to use the correction. Use HCD.19 for a material defect and HCD.7 or HCD.8 for a missing contribution.

#### HCD.23:4.4 - Choose a coherent interaction variant

The variants below depend on different contributions from the participants and the provider.

| Variant | What makes it useful | Condition that changes the choice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paired explanation of the same case | Each learner can inspect the full basis while testing a different account. | If both lack the prerequisite, provide preparation or competent help. |
| Team-Based Learning construction | Preparation, individual and team readiness work, feedback and application connect personal preparation with team judgement. | Use the coherent design when those contributions fit; a single group quiz does not supply the whole construction. |
| Jigsaw construction | Participants prepare different contributions with others working on the same part, then teach those contributions in their home groups before personal checking. | The parts must be teachable and join into an intelligible whole; a missing or unprepared explainer needs recovery. |

For a Jigsaw adaptation, establish how each part contributes to the whole and what its explainer must be able to answer. During expert-group preparation, check consequential misunderstandings before teaching the home group. If the explainer is absent, restore the group’s access to the qualified account and needed explanatory help where feasible, or identify the missing contribution. Report the learner’s missed explanation in that episode. When another opportunity is needed, use an adequate existing arrangement, organize one where feasible or state what prevents it. Receiving an answer sheet does not show that this learner practised explaining.

For a Team-Based Learning adaptation, preserve the point of the readiness work and the application challenge. Let participants use timely feedback to resolve a preparation gap; subsequent team decisions should require applying the relevant concepts. To report implementation of the whole design, check the additional contributions that define it. Consult the official design for the fuller sequence when using it.

#### HCD.23:4.5 - Return to a personal action and interpret it

When developing personal use, give each learner an attainable opportunity to apply the connection. For adaptation, change a decisive condition. For immediate correction, have the learner apply the feedback to the affected step and retry it when that is the learning purpose. State the permitted help, preserve any first response the claim needs and distinguish it from a later correction or justified retention. For completed work, use suitable surviving evidence. HCD.9 can help with feedback and a needed retry; HCD.11–HCD.13 address the corresponding performance, transfer or retention claim.

An explanation after discussion can show reconstruction under the help used. In an unfamiliar case, establish how the learner used the changed condition to justify an appropriate choice. The earlier action can remain warranted. Retention after a delay and a causal advantage of discussion need their own evidence. Finish with the finding, learning result or arrangement decision requested. If a needed contribution remains unavailable, identify the limit.

### HCD.23:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.23:5.1 - Agreement about a number conceals a different model

In this constructed case, two learners compare a release plan. The supplied rule requires two active specialist-hours per change and one further active hour for every batch of at most four changes. A 24-hour allowance is available. Both initially say ten changes fit. Learner A calculates twenty hours and omits batching; learner B calculates twenty plus three batch hours.

Their initial agreement conceals a consequential difference. B explains that ten changes take three batches. A reconstructs four, four and two and computes 23 specialist-hours. A asks whether setup takes active work or elapsed waiting. The rule counts active work. If the setup hours were unattended waits instead, ten changes would take 20 specialist-hours. Their elapsed completion time would also depend on the schedule.

The next personal task lowers the allowance to 22 hours. An answer of eleven changes from dividing by two fails the declared rule. Nine changes need eighteen plus three, or 21 hours; ten still need 23. The learner must change the proposed action and explain the batch count. If B supplies nine before A attempts the task, A’s correct number alone cannot establish who did the reasoning. A’s own explanation or calculation can show a reconstruction under that help. Use a suitable separate case or existing observation for a claim of independent adaptation.

Now suppose setup takes one active hour once for the entire run. With 22 hours, ten changes need 21 hours and eleven need 23. The earlier per-batch calculation would incorrectly rule out ten. Explain which assumption and reasoning changed. A correct number alone cannot show whether the learner used the changed rule.

#### HCD.23:5.2 - A missing explainer in an engineering studio

A studio uses a Jigsaw adaptation to compare three sensor arrangements. Each expert group prepares one arrangement’s measurement assumptions and failure conditions, then teaches its home group. The training case requires every reading of a known 10 mm displacement to fall within 1 mm of the reference. Its qualified case sheet gives these constructed observations and operating conditions for the three arrangements.

| Arrangement | Supplied result | Condition that changes its use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: optical path | 9.6–10.4 mm with a clear path | An opaque guard blocks the path; the case supplies no usable reading then. |
| B: shielded electrical arrangement | 9.5–10.5 mm under the stated interference | This qualification requires verified shield continuity. |
| C: unshielded electrical arrangement | 9.7–10.3 mm in the quiet condition; 8–12 mm with the motor energised | The changed interference condition violates the per-reading tolerance. |

C's prepared explainer is absent. In the receiving case the motor is energised and the optical path is blocked; B's shield continuity has been verified. A learner suggests averaging C's 8 and 12 mm readings to get 10. A substitute explainer uses the supplied criterion: the mean does not make either reading comply with the required 9–11 mm interval. B meets the per-reading requirement under the stated conditions; C is not qualified by its quiet-condition performance. The listener identifies both the condition and the failed criterion, then explains their own selection under the help received.

The instructor needs five minutes at 14:50–14:55 to check and supply C's permitted account and establish the replacement. Another prepared learner has finished their own home-group obligation by 14:45 and agrees to explain from 15:00 to 15:08. The three present recipients reserve 15:00–15:12: eight minutes for the explanation and questions, then four for each person's written selection and ground. Preparation and movement are complete before 15:00. Without the shared window or prepared substitute, this proposed recovery cannot supply the group’s explanation.

The absent learner’s practice is separate. At 16:00–16:15 the next day, the learner and one willing classmate have a booked qualified tutor. Five minutes are for the learner to explain the original criterion, five for the listener to pose a changed condition and five for feedback and the learner’s response. In the changed case the motor is off, the optical path is clear and B’s shield status is unknown. The learner qualifies A and C under their supplied bounds and identifies the missing shield-continuity evidence for B.

The additional allowance is twenty qualified provider-minutes: five for the first recovery and fifteen for later tutoring. The plan allows 74 learner-minutes: three recipients at twelve minutes, eight for the substitute, and fifteen each for the absent learner and returning classmate. Expert preparation is included in the original design. A late replacement, further preparation or a longer unresolved question changes the allowance. The first exchange can restore the group’s comparison. Use evidence of the absent learner’s later explanation and response to establish their contribution.

### HCD.23:6 - Bias-Annotation

Confidence and fluent terminology can accompany an unsupported account. A quiet learner’s prediction may show the decisive reasoning. Judge the action the task requires under the assistance present.

### HCD.23:7 - Conformance Checklist

- The exchange concerns a consequential connection with accessible subject criteria.
- Starting responses, preparation and visibility suit the question. Existing first responses may serve when their conditions match.
- Where the purpose requires use of another explanation, the task gives the learner a way to apply or test the grounds. Claims of completed use have evidence of that action.
- A disputed subject issue can be checked against its criterion or a qualified source, or reported as open.
- The selected personal return can show the target under the permitted help. For a finding about actual work, establish the learner’s contribution and what assistance was present and used.
- The chosen interaction variant includes the dependencies needed for its result.

### HCD.23:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

**Correct answer by assent.** Use evidence of the learner’s own reasoning to establish the connection they made. If that evidence is missing and a new observation is needed, provide an attainable opportunity and examine the learner’s response.

**Independent discovery before all teaching.** Supply preparation when a meaningful first attempt is unavailable.

**Disagreement settled by majority.** Return to the criterion and evidence.

**Every discussion needs a group report.** Keep a common report when the learning or working purpose needs it. A shared exchange can serve a different purpose on its own.

### HCD.23:9 - Consequences

A well-designed exchange gives participants an opportunity to reconstruct and use another account. Allow for accessible examples, qualified help and personal responses when planning that work. For an existing episode, use the available evidence of those contributions and their cost. An identified subject or support gap may answer the request without extending the discussion.

### HCD.23:10 - Rationale

Another person's answer can improve a product immediately. Connecting that answer to grounds, testing the connection and using it in a new action make the learner's contribution available for feedback. Preserving a changed-condition return helps distinguish a memorized result from a usable relation under the conditions of that task.

### HCD.23:11 - SoTA-Echoing

The [official Team-Based Learning account](https://www.teambasedlearning.org/learn-tbl) and [Jigsaw account](https://www.jigsaw.org/overview/) explain different preparations and dependencies for a coherent exchange. Use the construction that fits the task, or the part needed for an explicit adaptation as in §4.4.

The [collaborative cognitive-load account](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y) makes task complexity, preparation and coordination burden relevant to selection. Sections 4.1–4.2 retain explanation only when its contribution warrants that burden. [Bernstein, Shore and Lazer, 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6126746/) supplies a bounded reason to distinguish visibility from memory of one's own solution; its search experiment does not establish a universal teaching sequence.

Compared with immediate answer sharing, a learning exchange asks the recipient to reconstruct the grounds and, when the purpose requires it, apply them personally. It can start with teaching when the learners need preparation. Reconsider the exchange if learners already have the connection, it adds no useful contribution or required help is unavailable. The examples illustrate conditional reasoning. Attributing an educational effect to the exchange requires appropriate observations and a comparison that can support that attribution.

### HCD.23:12 - Relations

Use HCD.6 or HCD.6.1 for a needed task or distinction, HCD.20 or HCD.21 for arrangement or membership, and HCD.22 for shared-task dependence and visibility. Use HCD.9 when feedback or correction is needed. HCD.11–HCD.13 address stronger personal claims. Related learning may involve peer judgement under HCD.24 or use across projects under HCD.25. HCD.26 and HCD.27 address help with an ongoing exchange or the material and timing it needs. Use HCD.28 when these contributions must fit a whole product.

### HCD.23:End

## HCD.24 - Learn Evaluation and Revision through Peer Review

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner peer-review learning pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.24:0 - Use This When

Use this method to design or support learning through peer review, or to assess what a past exchange shows about a learner’s judgement or use of feedback. A collection of comments may leave the reviewer’s grounds unknown and the author unsure what to change or retain.

A **peer-review learning exchange** connects a reviewer’s judgement with an author’s response. Identify which participant’s action the task requires and how the design supports it or the existing work shows it. The author may adopt, adapt or reject advice, retain sound work or return an unresolved question. When an accepted issue calls for a change, distinguish the proposed response from the revised work. Publication, certification and production review keep their own criteria and authority.

Use permitted work the learners can understand, a usable criterion and help for uncertainty that matters. For a professional judgement on a work product, use an adequate existing review or obtain one from a qualified reviewer. To assess a learner’s evaluative judgement, establish which judgement the learner made and what help they used.

#### HCD.24:0.1 - Working Terms

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| criterion | The subject condition used to judge an identified part or property of the work. |
| calibration | Comparing judgements on common material with a qualified account of the criterion. Resolve differences that matter to the judgement, or identify the remaining disagreement. |
| comparative review | Judging one work using a comparable work to make a relevant difference discernible. |
| actionable feedback | A located issue or strength, its grounds and consequence, and an intelligible next action or reason to retain the work. |
| author response | The author explains why they adopt, adapt or reject feedback, or identifies an open question. When the response calls for a revision, the author makes it. Evidence of the revised work supports a claim that the repair was made. |

### HCD.24:1 - Problem Frame

A learner writes that a peer's analysis is clear and convincing. The analysis has selected a cause that its observations do not distinguish. A rubric naming correctness gives the learner a category but may not show how to inspect the missing inference. Later the author receives a score and cannot determine what to change.

When teaching both sides, make the criteria and relevant features accessible and give the reviewer and author opportunities to judge and respond. Include the time needed to read, compare, give feedback, respond, revise and resolve material disputes. Assess any saving in expert time separately from what the learners need to do.

### HCD.24:2 - Problem

How can peer review develop evaluative judgement and revision while giving the recipient useful feedback and preserving the competence and independence required by stronger decisions?

### HCD.24:3 - Forces

- Authentic work has consequential choices, while its background can exceed a peer's preparation or disclosure permission.
- A criterion constrains judgement, while its name alone may not make the decisive feature noticeable.
- Comparison can reveal a hidden difference, while incomparable tasks invite false ranking.
- Assistance improves feedback, while it can also supply the judgement whose acquisition is in question.
- An author should act on warranted criticism, while neither politeness nor majority agreement establishes its truth.

### HCD.24:4 - Solution

#### HCD.24:4.1 - Identify what each side is learning

Identify the reviewer’s learning target if there is one. It might be noticing a defect, applying a criterion, comparing alternatives, explaining a judgement or proposing a repair. On the author’s side it might be interpreting feedback, questioning a ground, revising or retaining a sound choice. Use HCD.6 for a representative task and HCD.11 when a later claim needs evidence of personal performance.

Select or use a bounded piece of work that exposes the target, with its purpose, constraints and permitted sources. A peer can judge whether a recommendation follows from the evidence given. Approving a project requires the relevant qualifications and authority. For a necessary question beyond the reviewer’s scope, use a qualified existing answer, refer the narrow issue to a capable provider when needed, or state what remains open.

Establish the shared or individual windows and qualified help needed for reading, review, an author’s response, any revision and consequential disputes. Use adequate existing arrangements. HCD.7 can help arrange missing support or identify a capacity limit. Estimate a potential saving in expert time from the proposed workloads; to report an actual saving, compare the work incurred under the relevant arrangements.

#### HCD.24:4.2 - Make the criterion usable

Explain how the criterion applies to the work. If its name leaves the decisive feature unclear, show a small contrast or use HCD.6.1 to construct one. To assess independent application, ask the learner to locate the feature and judge it before receiving a rationale that supplies the judgement. An eligible existing response can provide that evidence.

When calibration is needed, compare the learner’s grounds with the qualified account. Differences may reveal a misconception, ambiguous task information, a defective criterion or a legitimate alternative. Establish the supported explanation or indicate which ones remain open. A reviewer already applying the criterion adequately can proceed.

Give feedback on how the reviewer reached the judgement. If reviewers reach the same answer on incompatible grounds, examine the difference when it matters. If the reference answer is disputed, establish or correct its grounds, or state the limits on using it to judge learners.

#### HCD.24:4.3 - Choose and present comparable material

Use one work when its relevant property can be judged directly. When comparison makes a feature discernible, make the corresponding parts and their conditions available together, such as each observation, model assumption and recommendation. Establish whether the purposes support the comparison. Equal length or a common template leaves that question open.

Establish whether a difference warrants a different judgement on the selected criterion. A work may be preferable on one property and inadequate on another. Report equal or different judgements, legitimate alternatives or a supported finding that the works are incomparable. Identify a missing ground when the comparison remains unresolved.

In successive comparisons, reusing a familiar case can reduce rereading while introducing another contrast. Include reading and context switching in the budget. For long recordings, permitted aligned extracts may provide enough context. If abridgement hides the decisive relation, obtain a suitable representation, select an appropriate exercise or report the limit.

For confidential work, use a permitted fragment, a constructed counterpart preserving the target relation, or a qualified reviewer with the needed access. If a hidden assumption prevents the judgement, state the limit and any criterion that can still be applied. Use HCD.25 when transfer across projects is the question.

#### HCD.24:4.4 - Have the reviewer make and explain the judgement

The reviewer identifies the criterion, locates the passage or action and explains how its feature bears on the judgement. Tell the author what the grounds support, such as retaining a sound choice, checking a condition, correcting an inference or narrowing a claim. A well-grounded comment can leave the author to design the repair.

For example, “this conclusion is weak” gives neither the ground nor the next move. “The pressure is unchanged within the stated uncertainty, whereas this resistance explanation predicts an increase under your constant-efficiency assumption; revise the causal conclusion or supply a supported different account” identifies the discrepancy and a bounded action. The reviewer needs access to the subject assumptions on which that judgement rests.

For a new exercise, identify the judgement the learner must make before AI or another provider locates a passage, proposes wording or offers a counterexample. If independent judgement is at issue, preserve the first response before the decisive inference is shown. Later help can support a revision. For completed work, establish what the learner did, what help they received and what they used. A qualified supplied comment can directly serve the product-review task.

#### HCD.24:4.5 - Complete the author's side and resolve consequential disagreement

The author identifies the grounds for a comment and adopts, adapts or rejects it with a reason, or states what remains unresolved. If an accepted issue calls for revision, make the revision and keep enough of the earlier work to inspect what changed. A resolved flag can record disposition. To establish repair, examine the revised work.

For a consequential disagreement, align the task and criterion, then check which condition the author supplied and which one the reviewer inspected. Use a qualified existing source when it settles a question beyond the peers’ competence. If a prepared provider is needed and available, send the narrow question and relevant evidence. A protected decision belongs to its authorized holder. If the needed answer is unavailable, state what remains unresolved.

Return a consequential resolution to the affected participants. For an actual exchange, establish how the author changed or retained the work and how the reviewer corrected or retained their judgement, to the extent the question concerns each person. A correction with help supports the work done under that assistance. For a later independent performance claim, use a suitable independent case or existing evidence of one. Formal release, grading and authorization remain with their designated holders.

#### HCD.24:4.6 - Distinguish the resulting evidence

Report what the receiving question needs. Feedback produced, feedback used, improvement of the work, the reviewer’s demonstrated judgement and the author’s demonstrated ability to respond or revise can each have different evidence. Use HCD.9 when another attempt is warranted, HCD.11 for bounded performance and HCD.12 when transfer under a material change is in question.

Ungrounded comments or unusable feedback can reveal a learning need. For assurance, examine the qualified criterion, the relevant work, any comparison material, the participant contributions and help, and the author’s retained or revised work as the claim requires. Finish when the evidence answers the requested judgement or establishes its limit. If the assignment includes a repair, establish that the needed change was made before reporting completion. Reopen the affected use when a changed source, permission, criterion or learning requirement matters.

### HCD.24:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.24:5.1 - A correct ratio and an unsupported cause

This constructed exercise uses HCD.22's personal diagnostic case. Pressure is already measured at 400 ± 4 kPa; flow is 99.5 ± 1 m³/h and power 22.3 ± 0.2 kW, compared with the supplied baseline of 100 m³/h, 400 kPa and 20 kW. The task's qualified account states what the constant-efficiency resistance explanation would predict. No further worthwhile observation is obtainable within the case.

Work A correctly computes the approximate increase in the power-to-flow indicator, then recommends correcting increased resistance. Work B preserves the indicator change but says the unchanged pressure fails to support that simple explanation under its assumptions. The review criterion is whether the supplied evidence warrants the recommendation.

The reviewer first prefers A because it offers an action. During calibration the reviewer is asked what pressure A’s explanation predicts under its assumptions. Comparing the predicted pressure with the measurement exposes the missing inference. The reviewer asks the author to retain the arithmetic, withdraw the resistance-specific remedy and state the remaining explanation question and present limit.

The author accepts the mismatch but initially adds “take another pressure reading.” The reviewer points to the already obtained reading and exhausted useful-observation condition. The author replaces that instruction with a bounded conclusion and a return for a qualified alternative explanation if the receiving work requires one. A prepared mentor is available for any unresolved question about the subject model. A real plant intervention would need the appropriate operating authority.

The author revised the inference. The reviewer changed the initial preference for actionable-sounding text and applied the criterion with help. Preserve that distinction when judging the learning. Section 5.3 examines a case in which the recommendation stands. Include the preparation, time and qualified help each exchange requires in HCD.28’s product cost.

#### HCD.24:5.2 - When comparison cannot be made

Two internal teams offer material. One may disclose the full assumption-to-result passage. The other can disclose only its recommendation. The reviewer cannot inspect the grounds of the second recommendation. A permitted constructed counterpart can preserve the relation for learning, or the disclosed recommendation can be reviewed for clarity. Neither supplies a judgement on the undisclosed grounds of the second project.

#### HCD.24:5.3 - Retaining a warranted recommendation

A separate constructed instrument-check exercise supplies two reference values, 0 and 100 units, with a permitted error of ±1 unit. Repeated readings are 6 and 6 at the first reference and 106 and 106 at the second. The training procedure permits referral to a qualified calibration service after repeated checks outside tolerance. It does not require the learner to identify the failed component before making that referral, and it does not authorize the learner to adjust the instrument or declare it fit for return.

The author recommends the permitted referral and a new check before the instrument returns to use. The peer objects: “You have not distinguished a sensor fault from an electronics fault; withdraw the recommendation until you can.” The author accepts that the physical cause remains unknown but rejects the requested withdrawal. Both pairs of readings are six units above their references, outside the stated tolerance. The recommendation invokes the supplied referral criterion; it does not claim a component diagnosis or prescribe an adjustment.

A prepared instructor receives the disputed recommendation, readings and procedure. The narrow question is whether the missing component diagnosis defeats this next action. The instructor confirms that the referral criterion is met and explains the separate authority needed for adjustment and return. Both learners receive that resolution. The author retains the recommendation and its bounded ground. The reviewer withdraws the cause-demanding objection and replaces it with a supported judgement: the referral follows, while the cause and fitness after service remain to be established. The reviewer’s revised judgement provides evidence of using the referral criterion with the instructor’s help.

After the initial reading and comments, this example reserves ten minutes with both learners. Three minutes are for the author’s grounds, four with the prepared instructor, and three for the reviewer’s correction and author’s response. The resolution adds twenty learner-minutes and four instructor-minutes. Count initial preparation and review separately. If the instructor must reconstruct the procedure or the dispute persists, allow for the additional work or state what remains open. A later independent case can test the reviewer’s independent judgement when that is required.

### HCD.24:6 - Bias-Annotation

Politeness can suppress a warranted objection, and competitive ranking can turn criticism of a work into a judgement of the person. Apply the criterion to the work and its conditions. Use the reasoning or performance to assess a claim of improvement. Comment counts and lengths show how much commentary was produced. They do not establish that its inferences or the learner’s performance improved.

### HCD.24:7 - Conformance Checklist

- Identify which learning contribution is required of the reviewer, the author or both.
- The criterion is understandable and supported for the actual work.
- When works are compared, retain the context that makes their parts comparable.
- For a claim about the reviewer, establish the judgement they made, its grounds and the assistance they received or used. For independent judgement, establish that the decisive rationale had not already been supplied.
- For a claim about the author, establish their reasoned response and any revision the accepted issue required.
- For consequential disagreement, identify the qualified answer, a feasible way to obtain it or the issue that remains open.
- Feedback quality, product quality and personal learning claims remain distinguishable.

### HCD.24:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

**A rubric label teaches judgement.** Develop the decisive distinction and calibrate when needed.

**Treat a review as a popularity vote.** Judge the work using its criterion and evidence. If preferences are also relevant, establish whose preferences were expressed.

**Give a learner credit for an AI-generated judgement.** Establish which evaluative operation the learner performed and the help they used.

**The author must accept every comment.** Teach reasoned use, including warranted rejection.

**Count only savings in assessor time.** When learners are meant to judge work or use feedback, include the time and conditions those actions require. Retain qualified assessment where the product or decision needs it.

### HCD.24:9 - Consequences

A peer exchange can improve a work product and give either learner practice in judgement or revision. A disputed criterion may need a qualified source. A protected decision requires its authorized holder. Disclosure limits can prevent a comparison. Include the full burden of supplying the exchange when assessing its cost or feasibility.

### HCD.24:10 - Rationale

An evaluative distinction becomes useful when a learner can locate its evidence, explain the consequence and act on it. A recipient's reasoned response completes the feedback connection. Preserving both actions makes it possible to improve the teaching without reducing the exchange to a count of comments or an apparent saving in assessor time.

### HCD.24:11 - SoTA-Echoing

[Cambre, Klemmer and Kulkarni's Juxtapeer, 2018](https://d.ucsd.edu/srk/papers/2018/Juxtapeer-CHI2018.pdf) supplies aligned comparative review, overlapping pairs and feedback shown with its comparison context. Its reported feedback/reflection quality and ranking findings do not quantify learning gains or transfer. Sections 4.3–4.5 adapt that construction; calibration remains another useful option when learners need a qualified criterion before judging.

The [CMU Feedback Partner study, 2025](https://www.cmu.edu/teaching/gaitar/gaitaratscale/feedbackpartner.html) found no added writing benefit from giving two reviews on top of its AI-feedback condition. Use the study for the writing outcome it assessed. If learners need to develop reviewing judgement, give them an opportunity to apply the criterion and use evidence of their judgements under the stated conditions. Reconsider the exercise if it adds no needed learning contribution or if another supported arrangement serves the same target at lower full burden.

### HCD.24:12 - Relations

Use HCD.6 or HCD.6.1 for a needed representative task or discernible contrast, HCD.7 or HCD.8 for help, access or capacity, and HCD.9 for feedback or correction. HCD.11 addresses the relevant personal performance and HCD.12 transfer under a material change. HCD.23 develops mutual explanation and HCD.25 comparison across projects. Use HCD.20, HCD.21 or HCD.27 where grouping, contact or timing matters, and HCD.28 when incorporating the exchange and its costs into a whole product. Seek subject assessment from a competent source and a protected decision from the authorized holder.

### HCD.24:End

## HCD.25 - Learn Transfer through Comparison of Projects

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner cross-project learning pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.25:0 - Use This When

Use this method when learners need to recognize which part of a project’s reasoning or procedure can be used in another situation and where it would fail. A presentation may describe a local success while leaving the reason for its action hidden.

In a **learning comparison across project cases**, identify what warrants the action in each case and what result it supports. Test the correspondence by changing a condition that matters. A designer can supply a usable comparison or identify a missing condition. To assess a learner’s application, adaptation or warranted rejection, examine their work on the intended project or a permitted substitute, with its assumptions and the help they received.

Start with the target distinction or Method and qualified accounts of the cases. Supply the professional context needed to inspect the decisive relation. If the learners first encounter the target here, identify what the comparison is teaching. Assess their learning when the receiving question calls for that conclusion. For transfer of an earlier capability, establish its earlier basis and use the relevant HCD.12 comparison. If no permitted case preserves the relation, find a suitable source where feasible or identify the blocked use.

#### HCD.25:0.1 - Working Terms

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| project case | A bounded account of a work question, inputs, action and consequence, with enough context to judge the relevant relation. |
| correspondence | The proposed relation between parts of two cases that could justify adapting an operation. |
| breaking condition | A material change that defeats the grounds for carrying an action or conclusion from one case to another. The same action may still be warranted on a different basis. |
| own-case return | The learner's use, adaptation or warranted rejection of the proposed relation in their own work or a compatible permitted case. |

### HCD.25:1 - Problem Frame

An engineer, product manager and organiser discuss their projects. Each can describe a local success. Others copy a familiar phrase or a visible document format, but cannot say which inputs made the method appropriate. A novice may instead conclude that every unfamiliar project is incomprehensible and contributes nothing.

Choose a relation the learners can inspect. Give enough context to preserve the condition governing the target action and leave out professional detail the comparison does not use. Check that the simplified case still supports the local inference.

### HCD.25:2 - Problem

How can unlike projects supply a useful, bounded learning comparison that reaches a person's own action without treating similarity of stories or vocabulary as sufficient grounds for transfer?

### HCD.25:3 - Forces

- Unlike projects reveal different uses, while too many differences conceal the relevant relation.
- A concise case lowers reading cost, while omitted assumptions can make its conclusion unintelligible.
- Public discussion shares learning, while project owners may have limited disclosure rights.
- A common relation supports adaptation, while each domain retains criteria for whether its local action is warranted.
- A successful helped comparison supports learning, while a stronger transfer claim needs different evidence.

### HCD.25:4 - Solution

#### HCD.25:4.1 - Choose the learning question before allocating presentation time

State what the learner needs to recognize or adapt, such as when a calculation remains usable and when a changed condition needs new evidence. Identify the subject grounds and relevant preparation. Use HCD.6.1 when learners need a distinction made discernible. Use HCD.12 when the issue is transfer of an earlier contribution or application of a new source.

Choose cases that expose an important correspondence and a condition limiting it. Two may suffice. Add a case when it reveals another important condition, corrects a misleading cue or supplies evidence the learning question still needs. Allocation of presentation time is a separate participation decision.

Establish what participants must understand. A short explanation of quantities, participants or constraints may suffice. When the group lacks a necessary professional qualification, use or obtain a qualified account of the relevant step and retain the conditions under which it applies. Identify any comparison that remains unsupported.

#### HCD.25:4.2 - Obtain a permitted case that preserves the relation

Use a permitted account that identifies the project question, relevant inputs and conditions, the action proposed or taken, and its result or open consequence. An existing project record may supply them. If a material fact or permission is missing, identify a suitable source or holder and seek it when needed. Distinguish observed work from a constructed teaching case.

Check who may receive the material and for what use. An approved excerpt or a constructed analogue can preserve the target relation. Changing a client’s name may leave a workload dependency intact. Removing the workload can destroy it. Identify the constructed case and use it to teach the supplied relation. A conclusion about the undisclosed project needs evidence from that project.

Make both relevant parts accessible in a form learners can compare. Check what similarly named fields mean. If one result is a prediction and the other an observation, explain which inference each supports. Use HCD.7 for a needed access or support arrangement and HCD.24 when evaluative judgement is the learning target.

#### HCD.25:4.3 - Reconstruct the correspondence and try to break it

In a learning exercise, ask learners to explain which input or condition warrants the action in each case and which result that action can support. Then identify the proposed correspondence. For completed work, use the learner’s available explanation or application to establish the connection they made, and report a missing ground where relevant. Keep the source case and receiving use identifiable. Terms such as feedback and validation may name different operations in the two projects.

Examine what happens to the inference when a decisive condition changes. For example, retain the visible form but change the authorized effect of sending it, or change the format while retaining the operative rule.
