Ask whether the earlier action is warranted and on what grounds. HCD.6.1 can help construct a needed contrast.

Return the supported correspondence, its conditions or a warranted rejection. A model can remain usable while a particular installation needs new observations. Recalculating for different inputs does not establish those inputs. Rejecting an unsupported transfer can be the useful conclusion.

When participants disagree, identify the ground at issue. Use available project evidence or trace the condition directly. Ask a project holder or qualified specialist when they have the understanding, evidence or authority needed. If it is unavailable, state the supported part of the comparison and the unresolved connection.

#### HCD.25:4.4 - Return to personal work

When the learning task calls for personal application, have the learner identify the receiving question, name the conditions and carry out the bounded action. They may reuse a result, adapt an operation, obtain a needed observation or explain why the move is unavailable. If the actual project is closed, a permitted substitute can show what the learner did under its conditions. For a historical claim, identify what the learner did in the particular case.

Establish which premises and operations were supplied and which the learner obtained or devised. A missing prerequisite or a new subject Method may call for teaching or a qualified supplied result. Determine whether this was the obstacle before attributing failure to transfer of the original capability. Where feedback is needed, address the decisive correspondence. Use HCD.9 for a needed correction or reasoned retention.

For an independent transfer claim, use a case unfamiliar in the conditions that govern the action. In a new assessment, retain the learner’s first response before identifying the Method or decisive feature. For completed work, use suitable existing evidence of what the learner did, which resources were permitted and which help reached them. HCD.12 gives the full comparison and reporting conditions. An application with help can answer a learning question under those conditions.

#### HCD.25:4.5 - Retain what another learner can use

When the comparison is to be reused, retain a concise case where the relation holds, the condition that breaks it, the source or qualification that warrants the account, and the limits on sharing. Include enough context to reconstruct the grounds.

Return a material correction to the affected source or learning material. Retain cases whose grounds still hold. Recognize this need when project stories fail to show what carries into another situation. For stronger claims, use qualified accessible cases and evidence of the learner’s responses and conditions of use. Close with the result or limit for the selected question.

### HCD.25:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.25:5.1 - Repeating a calculation or obtaining another observation

Three adults in a distributed programme compare permitted fragments from their projects. The learning target is to distinguish a reused inference from new evidence about the world. The following facts and criteria are stipulated for the exercise.

| Case | Available basis | Receiving question and warranted move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: release capacity | A checked rule of two active hours per change plus one hour per batch of at most four, ten changes, 24 available hours and unchanged inputs | For another review of the same plan, reuse the checked 23-hour calculation on its stated conditions. Recalculating from those same inputs supplies no independent observation of capacity. |
| B: instrument installation | A qualified measurement from the previous installation and an available measurement procedure. A relevant installation condition has changed. | To judge the new installation, use applicable current evidence. If a new observation is needed, reuse the qualified measurement procedure where it applies. The old measurement still supports a question about the earlier installation. |

The learners notice that both projects have an earlier successful report. In A the rule and inputs for the capacity calculation still apply. B needs evidence of the present installation; the old measurement covers the former one. For another project, establish whether the conditions for using the earlier result still hold and what further evidence the receiving question requires.

Available specialist time in A falls to 22 hours. Ten changes still need 23 hours, so the plan no longer fits. Nine need three batches and 21 hours, so at most nine fit. This calculation uses the supplied rate; estimating a worker’s actual productivity would require observations of their work. If B asks only whether an earlier measurement was transcribed correctly, its original record can settle that use without a new installation observation.

In a personal exercise, two sensor reports trace to one observation. The participant identifies the common source and assesses whether it serves the question. If the criterion requires independent corroboration, another copy cannot meet it. Use a suitable independent observation already available, or seek one when it can be obtained and its expected contribution warrants the cost. If the required observation is unavailable, identify that limit. For a question about whether the two reports share a source, the provenance can already settle the matter.

The organizer examines the learner’s correspondence and next action against the supplied conditions. The sensor specialist is responsible for the measurement criteria. A cue identifying the common source makes a subsequent correction a helped response. Keep an earlier independently supported answer distinct if the learner had already reached it. The exercise supplies a design and conditional answers. A claim about real transfer needs evidence of the learner’s work and conditions relevant to that claim.

#### HCD.25:5.2 - The decisive project fact cannot be shared

An internal team cannot disclose the installation condition that makes B's earlier observation inapplicable. Removing it produces a case with no visible reason to obtain new evidence. The organiser uses a permitted constructed installation change and tells participants that it is a teaching case. Learners can practise the relation on that case; the group does not claim to have diagnosed the closed installation.

If no permitted analogue retains the relation, use another suitable case, arrange a qualified private learning exchange with the necessary access when feasible, or report why the public comparison cannot establish the connection.

#### HCD.25:5.3 - Repeating a request without repeating its effect

Three learners compare a software integration with a print-production project. The question is when repeating a request after a lost acknowledgement preserves the intended result. The cases stipulate the local operating rules for learning this relation. To establish earlier independent transfer, evidence of the learners’ earlier and receiving work would be needed.

| Project account | What repetition does under the supplied conditions |
| --- | --- |
| Software service | An allowed HTTP PUT replaces one identified image with the supplied content. With the same target, identical content and no intervening writer, retrying after the lost response leaves the intended image state the same. The bounded idempotence account in [RFC 9110, §9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2) allows different responses or additional logs. |
| Print workshop | The exercise gives each authorized run one work card. A status inquiry on the same completed card returns its completion notice and cannot start another run. Submitting a new card requests another run, even with identical artwork. |

The learners reconstruct the local mechanisms. In the service, repeating the specified update can leave the identified image in the required state whether the first attempt completed or failed. In the workshop, querying an existing run may establish its status. Submitting a new card can start another run. The correspondence depends on what each authorized operation does under the receiving conditions. A filename or printed job number alone supplies no such rule.

Now suppose the workshop treats every submitted form as a new run and has no operation for reopening the earlier card. Submitting the same form again could print a second batch. Reject that repeat instruction. Use the available job evidence or ask the operator when their account or action is needed. If the status cannot be established and no authorized operation can safely deliver the required result in every still-possible state, leave the run open. Apply the receiving service’s own rules to a software retry as well.

In a permitted rehearsal, an event producer must resolve a lost acknowledgement for cue C7. Each console trigger plays the sound, and the operator can inspect the playback log. The learner proposes triggering C7 again. Asked to trace the effect, they instead request the status of that occurrence. The log shows completion; the learner asks the operator to confirm it and leaves the single playback in place. If the log is inconclusive, another trigger could duplicate the sound. Refer that uncertainty to the responsible operator. These constructed responses illustrate a helped correction. Claims about a real learner’s transfer or sound-engineering competence require their own evidence.

The three case owners each need ten preparation minutes to qualify their bounded account; the organiser needs twelve to align the fragments. Three learners each read for eight minutes before a shared thirty-minute exchange: twelve for the first comparison, seven for their own first responses, six with the prepared provider for the consequential question, and five for individual corrections. The facilitator is booked for all thirty minutes and the provider for the six-minute help interval. The allowance is 78 provider-minutes including preparation, and 114 learner-minutes. If one provider covers overlapping assignments within the booked window, count that person’s time once. Check that the combined duties fit. Missing prerequisites, permissions or a longer unresolved question change the allowance. Learners use the supplied local mechanisms; specialists retain responsibility for implementing and qualifying the real service, workshop and console.

### HCD.25:6 - Bias-Annotation

Familiar vocabulary can conceal a different operation. Unfamiliar detail can conceal a usable relation. Identify the professional knowledge the comparison needs and use evidence of the learner’s own application before attributing transfer.

### HCD.25:7 - Conformance Checklist

- A named learning operation determines case selection.
- Each permitted case retains its decisive local grounds.
- The compared actions or relations and their local grounds are identifiable.
- A change to a decisive condition tests the grounds for carrying an operation or conclusion into another case.
- In a design, identify the intended opportunity for personal application. For a performance claim, establish what the learner did in their own case or in a permitted substitute, and retain the conditions and limits of that evidence.
- New learning, helped application and transfer of an earlier contribution are distinguished.
- Preserve the source, permission and material limits needed to reuse the comparison.

### HCD.25:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

**Every project gets the same presentation slot.** Select and prepare the cases needed for the current comparison.

**All projects share a pattern name.** Reconstruct what corresponds and what would invalidate the move.

**Anonymization removed the decisive condition.** Use a permitted counterpart that preserves the relation, change the task or identify the comparison that remains unavailable.

**A new source was learned, so prior transfer succeeded.** Use the matching HCD.12 question and evidence.

### HCD.25:9 - Consequences

A project comparison can make a local operation usable in another field or show why the proposed transfer fails. Include the preparation, permissions and feedback the learning question requires. Claims about broader professional competence need grounds at that scope.

### HCD.25:10 - Rationale

Explain which relation warrants the operation and what changes when its decisive condition changes. When personal application is in question, examine the learner’s work with the resources permitted and the help they received. Use qualified grounds for the subject action. Carrying its relation into a learning exercise leaves any real implementation or approval with the responsible practitioners.

### HCD.25:11 - SoTA-Echoing

HCD.6.1 explains how varying a decisive condition or an incidental cue can make a distinction discernible. HCD.12 distinguishes prior transfer from learning with a new source. Use the contribution the learning question needs. Here the practitioner selects permitted cases from different projects, makes the local relations intelligible and arranges personal application where required.

Juxtapeer's [comparative-review construction](https://d.ucsd.edu/srk/papers/2018/Juxtapeer-CHI2018.pdf) is a related bounded example of making comparable parts available together; its findings do not establish professional transfer. Compared with unstructured project presentations, §§4.2–4.4 add a recoverable relation and a breaking condition at a real preparation cost. Retain ordinary presentation when sharing information is the actual purpose. Reconsider the learning comparison when a simpler example suffices, the cases cease to be comparable, or the receiving work needs another subject Method.

### HCD.25:12 - Relations

Use HCD.6.1 to construct a needed contrast and HCD.6 for the selected action in meaningful practice. Use HCD.12 for the corresponding transfer or new-source question, HCD.23 for explanatory exchange and HCD.24 for evaluative review. Use HCD.7 or HCD.8 for missing access or competent support, HCD.21 for participant selection and HCD.27 for compatible preparation and return windows. HCD.28 includes the comparison when the product requires it.

### HCD.25:End

## HCD.26 - Regulate Shared Learning

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner shared-regulation pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.26:0 - Use This When

Use this method when a group needs to establish how a shared learning attempt is going or change how it proceeds. The question may have drifted, a necessary contribution may be absent, one answer may have displaced others’ reasoning or the available help may no longer fit the difficulty. An existing observation may also answer a question about how a past attempt was regulated.

In **regulating a shared learning attempt**, compare the intended contribution with what the group is doing. Make a consequential difference accessible to those who can act on it. Where a response is needed, choose a feasible one and examine the subsequent work. A dashboard, reflection prompt or facilitator comment may help. For a historical question, establish which of those actions occurred. Individual self-regulation and ordinary workplace coordination have their own practices.

Return a supported account of the attempt, a checked continuation, a justified request for help or a reason to pause. An adequately progressing group can continue. When the difficulty concerns a subject Method, use a qualified subject result, seek needed help or state which inference remains open.

#### HCD.26:0.1 - Working Terms

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| shared intention | The result and required contributions the group presently understands itself to be pursuing. |
| actual state | What has been attempted, obtained, misunderstood or left unavailable at the scope relevant to the inquiry or next action. Use the available evidence to establish what is known about it. |
| process cue | A question or suggestion about how to continue the work. Identify separately any subject answer the intervention also supplied. |
| uptake | What participants did with a cue: they may use, adapt or reject it. To establish uptake, examine their response. Evidence of delivery or display alone may leave their use unknown. |
| checked continuation | A next action supported by the observed work. It can retain an adequately progressing course. When a regulation move was made, inspect the relevant work after it to assess its consequence. |

### HCD.26:1 - Problem Frame

Four participants intend to compare model grounds. Halfway through the meeting, they are editing the wording of one person's answer. Each is busy, the shared document is growing and the intended reasoning remains unperformed. A facilitator can interrupt, but a generic instruction to collaborate better may be ignored or consume the remaining time.

Make enough of the work accessible to answer the question. Comparing the next required contribution with the actual response may suffice in a short discussion. If a change is needed, identify what participants can do within the available time, access and competence.

### HCD.26:2 - Problem

How can a group recognize a consequential deviation, choose proportionate process help and determine whether that help restored the learning work?

### HCD.26:3 - Forces

- A shared view supports coordination, while extensive reporting displaces the learning itself.
- Timely prompting can restore a missing action, while interruption can break a productive explanation.
- A facilitator can detect a difficulty, while participants need to acquire the ability to notice and act themselves when that is a target.
- A process problem and a subject problem can look alike, while their remedies differ.
- Participation data can expose a missing contribution, while speaking frequency alone says little about its value.

### HCD.26:4 - Solution

#### HCD.26:4.1 - Make the intended work recoverable

Make the common question, needed contributions and next useful result recoverable during the attempt. A sentence and an accessible case may suffice. For longer work, keep any unresolved decision and responsibility for each necessary contribution available to the participants. For a past attempt, use the evidence of what they were pursuing and could access. Limit disclosure to what coordinating the action needs.

Establish how participants can request a pause, report missing information or challenge the course. Use a suitable existing agreement or help the participants settle the missing condition. Clarify what the facilitator or tool can observe and supply. A group expecting a subject answer from a bot may misunderstand a process cue. Use HCD.7 when help or access needs arranging.

Choose an observation occasion when a dependency matters, such as before adopting a model, when a contribution is due or when progress stalls. A scheduled check can help an inexperienced group. Retain or remove it in light of how participants recognize and handle that occasion under the needed conditions.

#### HCD.26:4.2 - Compare actual work with the intention

Compare the contribution needed with the evidence of work so far, such as an unexplained step, a response to a changed condition, a missing annotation or an unresolved question. Attendance and transcript volume can establish presence or amount of talk. To establish reasoning, examine the relevant explanation or action.

Distinguish explanations that change the requested finding or a possible remedy. A quiet participant may be reasoning, lack a usable channel, feel unable to challenge a supervisor or lack a prerequisite. Use available evidence of the required contribution and its conditions. If the contribution is still needed, ask for it; seek the participant’s own account when their experience matters. Check why a revised question may now serve the group before restoring an older plan.

“We have the ratio but no account connecting it to a cause” locates a missing inference. An impression of disengagement leaves its cause open. If access is the obstacle, report that finding or restore access when the task requires it and a remedy is feasible. If the criterion is defective, identify the affected conclusion and send the defect to whoever can correct the criterion when correction is needed. Use HCD.14 for a question about revising an individual’s development arrangement.

#### HCD.26:4.3 - Select the smallest feasible regulation move

When an intervention is needed, choose the smallest feasible change that addresses the established difficulty while preserving productive work. The table links possible moves to the work that can show their use.

| Observed difference | Possible process move | What must then be inspected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One account has displaced a needed comparison | Ask another participant to reconstruct its decisive ground and test it against a credible rival or breaking condition. | What that person did with the ground, and whether the comparison supports, changes or limits the conclusion. |
| Two participants use different task assumptions | Pause selection and align those assumptions. | Whether the remaining disagreement still exists under the same conditions. |
| A needed contribution has not arrived | Restore access to the source, use a qualified substitute, reassign feasible work or request help as appropriate. If the contribution remains unavailable, identify the limit. | What reached the next participant in usable form, and whether anyone missed a required learning opportunity. |
| A prompt repeatedly interrupts useful reasoning | Let the current connection finish. Adjust or remove the trigger when justified. | Whether the group now notices the relevant difficulty and can continue without the interruption. |
| The required personal action does not fit the remaining time | Narrow the present result or arrange a feasible later window. Report a needed action that cannot be scheduled. | Whether the revised plan provides the time, access and help it requires. |

Make the cue intelligible in relation to the actual work. “Before choosing resistance, which observation distinguishes it from the other account?” may reveal a missing question. To complete the comparison, the group also needs the criterion or a qualified way to obtain it. If that is the missing contribution, repeated reminders leave it unavailable.

Count the intervention within the actual window. A two-minute pause may fit early in the session and miss a later deadline. Preserve protected work when reducing other demands. If it cannot fit, return the limit or use HCD.27 to arrange a feasible later continuation. Report completion from the actions performed.

#### HCD.26:4.4 - Inspect uptake and consequence

For an intervention already made, examine the next relevant work. Establish whether participants used, adapted, rejected or ignored the cue, or whether the evidence leaves their response unknown. Check what the next action required and what the participants did. A delivery record shows delivery. Repeating a phrase may show imitation without the reasoning the task required.

If a cue appears to have been ignored, establish what reached participants, whether they understood it and whether it suited the work and timing. If the group has already resolved the issue, withdraw an obsolete cue. Clarify a misunderstood cue or address a task or support defect when useful and feasible. Add another prompt only when it can supply a contribution still needed. An account of a finished attempt can end with the established reason or limit.

A prompt may elicit the missing question while leaving the subject answer open. Report that partial gain. If the answer matters, use qualified help that is available or worth obtaining. If an interruption disrupts productive work, resume it where feasible and reconsider the trigger.

#### HCD.26:4.5 - Make regulation available to participants

If participants need to regulate later work themselves, make the occasion, observed difficulty and grounds for the facilitator’s action intelligible. Give participants a feasible opportunity to notice a comparable occasion, choose a response and inspect its consequences. Use evidence of their actual work to decide whether to reduce the external cue.

A group may need occasional external help. For reliable work with a facilitator, establish the required help, access and cost. To claim independent regulation, observe the relevant contribution without the help that would supply it, or use adequate evidence of such work. Use OCE when the subject is the capability of a workplace team.

A regulation question arises when the intended and observed learning work diverge or their relation needs checking. To report uptake or the work that followed, use evidence of the corresponding action. To claim that an intervention improved the work, compare the relevant outcomes on grounds that support that attribution. Close when the finding or continuation is supported within its stated limits.

### HCD.26:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.26:5.1 - A useful question that is first ignored

In a constructed thirty-minute diagnostic discussion, four participants should compare rival accounts and return to personal model selection. At minute twelve the shared page contains one person's conclusion and stylistic edits by the others. The facilitator asks which observation distinguishes that account from the rival. Participants nod and continue editing.

The continued editing shows that the group did not use the requested comparison at this point. A short clarification reveals that participants can calculate the indicator but lack the pressure implication. The facilitator supplies the permitted subject reference and asks two learners to relate its prediction to the reading. The others explain the resulting limit. The group preserves the arithmetic and revises the causal statement with that help. The episode leaves its earlier independent command of the criterion open.

The facilitator used part of the booked help window for clarification and checks the time left for the planned personal action. If explanation and reconciliation need fifteen minutes and ten remain, the group cannot deliver the original result in that window. It keeps the supported work and uses or arranges a feasible later window for the missing action if still needed, or reports the limit.

A two-minute explanation after this first episode makes the facilitator's ground available: the page changed, but no participant had connected a predicted observation to a cause. The group identifies the next comparable occasion just before committing to a causal recommendation. The pressure criterion remains accessible. They agree to try noticing that occasion themselves; qualified subject help remains available.

In the next constructed twenty-minute case, the facilitator withholds the scheduled process cue. At minute six a participant notices that a preferred cause has again become the common answer without its predicted observation. Another adapts the earlier question into “write the prediction first, then compare it with the reading.” Two minutes for personal predictions and four for comparison expose the decisive relation. Using the case's supplied resistance prediction, one learner writes 448 kPa against the supplied 400 ± 4 kPa observation and withdraws the resistance-specific remedy; the other three also connect their judgement to the supplied condition instead of polishing the first answer. Five minutes remain for personal returns and three to inspect whether the comparison occurred and whether the cue helped. The group has supplied the occasion, adapted the move and inspected its consequence without the scheduled interruption. Repeating the phrase without those actions would leave the original difficulty.

The following twenty-minute case tests the limit. At minute four the group notices that the machine's current operating condition is missing, so the earlier pressure account cannot yet be applied. They reject an immediate “compare the predictions” cue because the case lacks the operating condition the comparison needs. During minutes four to six they prepare the narrow question for the qualified provider booked from minute six to twelve. The provider confirms that the available case cannot establish the operating condition and that no further observation is available within this exercise. The participants therefore change their shared question from choosing a remedy to stating the supported conclusion and the missing input that prevents the choice. Each writes that bounded return in minutes twelve to seventeen; in the remaining three they inspect whether it preserves the useful calculation and the reason to withhold a cause-specific remedy. A changed question now serves the task better than restoring the original demand.

For this familiar decision point, the two cases support withdrawing the scheduled process cue while retaining accessible criteria and qualified subject help. The observed actions concern these occasions under those conditions. An independent-team claim needs evidence from the intended operating situation. If participants again miss the decision point or their cue displaces personal work, restore the smallest support that addresses the difficulty and examine its use. An adequate attempt can continue.

For this extension, preparation takes twelve facilitator-minutes to build the two cases and six subject-provider-minutes to qualify their accounts. The two-minute explanation, both twenty-minute facilitator bookings and the six-minute subject-help booking bring the added total to 66 provider-minutes. The allowance for four learners is 42 minutes each for the explanation and both cases, or 168 learner-minutes. Reading the new cases is inside their opening work intervals. These allowances are additional to the first episode. The facilitator remains booked while observing the participant-led attempts, so fewer spoken cues do not yet establish a staff-time saving. Further teaching, unavailable help or an unresolved condition changes the arrangement. The trajectory is constructed to expose the decisions and their evidence; it is not an observed learning-effect result.

#### HCD.26:5.2 - A quiet equipment observer

In an internal training team, one participant operates a safe instrument and another watches silently. A talk-frequency dashboard flags low participation. Before prompting speech, the facilitator asks for the task's required prediction. The observer points out the unexpected reading and requests the planned pause. The observer has supplied the required contribution. Additional commentary could interrupt the observation.

If the observer cannot access the reading, restore suitable access where feasible or identify the limit. If the reading is accessible but its significant difference is unclear, use a suitable existing contrast or construct one with HCD.6.1. The same silence under different conditions therefore leads to different actions.

### HCD.26:6 - Bias-Annotation

Facilitators may favor familiar interventions and tools may privilege what they can count. Judge the response by the contribution the task requires. Use a shared display when it makes a needed question or condition visible at an acceptable reporting cost.

### HCD.26:7 - Conformance Checklist

- Establish the intended result and consequential contributions. For live coordination, make them recoverable by the participants. For a past attempt, use the available evidence of what the group understood and identify any remaining uncertainty.
- Identify the relevant difference, the grounds for keeping the present course, or the condition that prevents a judgement on this attempt.
- Match a proposed remedy to the process, subject, access or timing condition it addresses. Record a consequential condition that remains open.
- For a proposed cue or change, check that it fits the available work window. When examining a past cue, establish whether it fitted and what that meant for the task.
- For a claim about what happened, establish uptake and subsequent work to the extent the claim requires.
- Any claim about participant regulation distinguishes it from facilitator performance.

### HCD.26:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

**Credit delivery as uptake.** Use the delivery record for delivery. For a claim of regulation, examine how participants responded and what followed.

**Repeat until obeyed.** Check relevance, comprehension, timing and missing inputs.

**Measure collaboration by speech count.** Look for the required contribution.

**Remove help on a fixed date.** Adjust assistance using evidence about the required performance, or retain an adequate supported arrangement.

### HCD.26:9 - Consequences

The group can locate a difficulty and recover useful work, or establish that its present course is adequate. A poorly timed intervention can consume the window needed for learning. Assess the cost and expected contribution when introducing, changing or withdrawing a cue.

### HCD.26:10 - Rationale

A mismatch matters when it changes the learning contribution, the grounds for judging it or the feasible next action. Making the difference visible can give participants an opportunity to respond. To assess what happened, trace the group’s or facilitator’s action to the subsequent work. When the question concerns a cue, establish how the participants used, adapted, rejected or ignored it, or what the available evidence leaves open.

### HCD.26:11 - SoTA-Echoing

[Edwards et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13534) supplies a bounded design line connecting awareness, externalization and process prompting. The study involved 52 pre-service teachers in 14 groups; trained humans simulated proactive voice intervention, while a separate reactive chat used GPT-4. It found no significant increase in lexical alignment following prompts, and its revised prompt design remained a proposal.

Sections 4.1–4.4 adapt the relation between awareness, prompting and subsequent work. To report uptake or a consequence, examine the corresponding evidence. Compared with an automatic reflection prompt, the intervention is selected from the work; compared with unassisted continuation, it can supply a missing occasion or question. Coordination burden and task preparation from the [collaborative cognitive-load account](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y) constrain that choice. Reconsider the trigger when it is ignored, disrupts useful action or addresses the wrong cause. Neither cited account validates the constructed cases or establishes an autonomous agent's equivalent performance.

### HCD.26:12 - Relations

Use HCD.22 to design or assess the shared task, HCD.23 for explanatory work or HCD.24 for evaluative work when needed. Use HCD.7 or HCD.8 for help and HCD.14 for a question about revising an individual arrangement. HCD.21 can assess or change membership, and HCD.27 can restore compatibility of timing and materials. HCD.28 uses regulation requirements and costs when they affect the whole product. Use OCE for workplace team capability or operating coordination.

### HCD.26:End

## HCD.27 - Coordinate Personal Learning Routes with a Shared Rhythm

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner learning-route coordination pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.27:0 - Use This When

Use this method to examine or coordinate the connection between personal preparation, a shared learning episode and each learner’s subsequent work. A common timetable can leave a discussion without usable material or feedback too late to use. Different learners may need different preparation or recovery opportunities.

In **coordinating personal learning routes and shared episodes**, identify what each person must prepare, what reaches the shared work and what returns to their practice or next task. Shared occasions need compatible contributions and windows. Participants can prepare at different speeds or join different groups when the learning task allows it.

Return the route and what its conditions permit, a specific material or timing gap, or a feasible arrangement for the required continuation. When asked about completed work, establish the transfers, exchanges or personal actions the question concerns. Use an individual programme and suitable support for a task without a shared dependency. If the team must later work together in its workplace, establish that operating rhythm with the relevant organization and work methods as well.

#### HCD.27:0.1 - Working Terms

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| shared episode | An occasion at which participants need compatible contributions for a learning action. |
| entry condition | The preparation, material, access and time that make the person's intended contribution possible. |
| material transfer | Selection or transformation of an actual result into usable input for the next participant or activity. |
| return window | Time, access and qualified help where needed for using feedback, retaining or correcting an answer, or re-entering work. |
| re-entry | Resuming from what the learner has already achieved. For a proposed return, establish a feasible way to supply any contribution still needed. For a completed one, establish what was restored and how the learner resumed. |

### HCD.27:1 - Problem Frame

A paid distributed programme assigns annotations before a meeting. Some participants submit conclusions without grounds; others have not received the source. The meeting proceeds through a generic presentation, and everyone is marked as having completed the collaborative task. Later, all revised work arrives in the same hour, exceeding the assessor's available attention.

A separate programme for every learner can multiply preparation and lose useful exchanges. Share the work that benefits from synchrony and allow different preparation, depth or recovery where needed. Test each connection by what the receiving activity can use.

### HCD.27:2 - Problem

How can individual routes and shared episodes stay compatible when preparation, access, pace and support needs differ, without hiding missing actions or infeasible feedback demand?

### HCD.27:3 - Forces

- A common window concentrates useful exchange, while it also concentrates demand and excludes some personal schedules.
- Different preparation calls for different entry support, while unlimited individual exceptions can make the service infeasible.
- Asynchronous work can fit personal time, while a subsequent conversation needs material of usable meaning and quality.
- Recovery preserves learning opportunity, while a summary cannot replace every missed interaction.
- Shared preparation can save provider work, while checking and correction may remain personal.

### HCD.27:4 - Solution

#### HCD.27:4.1 - Identify the dependencies that require coordination

Start with the personal targets and the contribution the shared episode needs. Use existing target and task information, or HCD.20 and HCD.22 when comparing arrangements or designing a shared task is still needed. Establish what each episode receives and what it returns. Learners can work at different speeds or on different examples while producing compatible inputs. Distinguish required common preparation from optional depth.

For a future audience, establish the entry conditions and assumptions the product design needs, using HCD.28 where appropriate. For known people, use evidence of their work, preparation, access and participation constraints. HCD.2 can help when an individual programme is at issue. The same person may be prepared for one contribution and need support for another.

Coordinate timing where it enables the contribution. Independent reading before a common discussion can start at different times. For practice in answering a live challenge, the learner needs an actual exchange. For an inquiry into a past attempt, a transcript that captures the learner’s challenge and response may establish what occurred. Reading someone else’s transcript cannot supply one’s own live response.

#### HCD.27:4.2 - Construct the material connection

Identify what the receiving activity must use. For example, a model comparison may require an observation, candidate explanation, decisive assumption and any open question. Give producers the requirements, timing, accessible format and reason for the needed parts. When assessing an existing route, check what the actual instructions and materials make available.

Identify any selection or transformation needed for the next use. A facilitator may group annotations by conflicting assumptions, select a pair that exposes a shared difficulty or obtain a permitted extract with its source context. Preserve the personal responses needed for later work. An annotation omitted from the common selection may still need individual feedback; retain that need when planning the service.

For a completed transfer, establish what arrived and whether the recipient could use it in time. For a proposal, check whether delivery and access are feasible. If grounds are missing, use an adequate existing source or ask for the missing part while it can still be supplied. A prepared case, changed question or later episode may restore the shared work. Identify which contribution the substitute supplies and which intended learning opportunity, if any, is still missing.

For a design, specify what the shared episode should return and how each learner can use the result in their next work. It may be a clarified condition, a supported or corrected account, a question for a specialist or a next action. For a completed exchange, establish what was returned; when actual use is claimed, identify what the learner did with it. A recording may preserve context. A concise, supported answer can spare the learner from reconstructing it.

#### HCD.27:4.3 - Make preparation, help and correction fit

On the relevant horizon, locate preparation, exchange, feedback, any needed correction or check, and the later action that needs the result. Use existing information about access, competence and capacity, or HCD.7 when the support arrangement needs work. Check peak demand against the same availability windows for learners and providers. A visit must receive its inputs in time and return its answer before use. Include movement, connection, coordination and recovery where they require time.

When a window fails, identify the shortfall. If a remedy is requested, compare feasible alternatives that affect the choice, such as staggering submissions, adding competent assessors, choosing another shared time, reducing optional work or changing the promise. If a required personal check is shortened, state how that changes the learning or assurance result. Where no acceptable remedy is available, report the limit.

For an entry gap that can be closed in time, offer or use the bounded preparation the learner needs when the task includes provision. A learner who already meets the condition can proceed to the intended work or a useful extension. If preparation exceeds the available time or resources, qualify a different occasion or arrangement where needed, or report the unsupported entry. Include any additional preparation in the timetable and product cost before offering it.

For asynchronous work, identify the response windows, partners, providers or material transfers the particular activity needs. For a synchronous exchange, establish that participants can attend together. Compare active learner time, provider work and elapsed delay separately when the difference matters.

#### HCD.27:4.4 - Restore a missed contribution and resume from supported work

After a missed occasion, establish which contribution, if any, is missing. It might be information, an opportunity to explain, a response to the learner’s work or an assessment. A summary can restore information. Dialogue or a first independent judgement needs the conditions of that action. If restoration is needed, use the smallest feasible replacement that supplies the missing contribution, or report the limit.

Keep valid completed work and identify the next unfinished action when a continuation is needed. Re-establish any changed criterion, source, permission or help condition before relying on it. Use HCD.21 if a new partner is needed. A later exchange can restore an opportunity to explain; a contrasting case with suitable feedback may serve individual practice. Interpret resulting observations under the assistance and conditions that applied.

When a learner needs to return, establish the required conditions and whether a suitable window exists. If one exists, identify it. Otherwise report the gap and any feasible alternative. Repeated recovery demands may justify reassessing the common schedule or support. Use HCD.20 for the affected arrangement, HCD.28 for the product or HCD.7 for missing support. Retain independently usable parts.

#### HCD.27:4.5 - Revise the rhythm from its actual use

Use evidence of what arrived, which exchanges occurred, whether feedback could be used in time and what coordination or recovery required. Distinguish problems of material, preparation, access and provider delay. HCD.26 addresses a live shared attempt and HCD.14 the affected person’s arrangement. When a mismatch recurs across the intended audience, use HCD.28 to examine the reusable product; a single observed failure needs its own warranted scope.

One failed connection can identify the need, such as annotations that cannot support a meeting. To qualify a planned route, establish its requisite inputs, access and support windows. To report what happened or what a learner did, use evidence of the work under its actual conditions. Close with the supported finding, feasible continuation or specific remaining limit.

### HCD.27:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.27:5.1 - A distributed adult programme with a real return

This constructed additional block has twelve adults comparing the use of evidence in permitted project fragments. It is separate from HCD.28's diagnostic product. Each learner prepares a short question, ground and conditional conclusion asynchronously; three groups of four will compare selected cases on Wednesday evening.

The initial design promises feedback on twelve fragments between 13:00 and 14:00 Tuesday. At eight assessor-minutes per fragment the work needs 96 minutes, while one assessor has 60. The provider confirms a two-hour window, reserving 96 minutes for checking and feedback and 24 for unexpected clarification. If that window is unavailable, the designer must obtain adequate qualified capacity or change the sequence or promise before offering it.

| Occasion | Material or action that becomes available | Next use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tuesday noon | Twelve permitted fragments are due with their decisive grounds. | The assessor checks what arrived in the confirmed 13:00–15:00 window and can identify missing grounds. |
| Tuesday 15:00–15:20 | The facilitator selects three contrasting pairs, preserving relevant source conditions | Each group is due a pair it can compare under the stated source conditions. |
| Before Wednesday 18:00 | Learners read the selected pair and use the returned feedback to supply missing grounds or retain supported ones. | The meeting can compare reasoning that has reached the group in usable form. A permitted prepared contrast may supply the comparison if some original grounds remain missing. |
| Wednesday, group starts 18:00, 18:08 and 18:16 | Each group performs the thirty-minute sequence below; one prepared mentor visits at 18:18, 18:26 and 18:34 | Each learner has time to use the qualified response in explaining their retained or revised grounds. |
| Thursday noon | Personal applications to a changed own or substitute case | The assessor checks the twelve returns in another confirmed two-hour window with the same 96-minute demand and 24-minute reserve. |
| Friday noon, then 13:00–14:00 | Learners submit any needed corrections by noon. The assessor has 48 minutes for up to twelve four-minute checks and reserves twelve minutes for unresolved help. | The result states what is supported. Demand beyond the reserve requires another suitable confirmed window or a stated limit. |

The Wednesday mentor is booked from 18:16 to 18:46. The groups have confirmed different starts, with the following joint allocation. All four initial judgements take twelve minutes, peer comparison takes six, qualified help takes six, and each learner has ninety seconds within the final six to explain what they will keep or revise.

| Group | Initial judgements, 4 × 3 min | Peer comparison | Subject help | Personal retained or revised grounds, 4 × 1.5 min |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 18:00–18:12 | 18:12–18:18 | 18:18–18:24 | 18:24–18:30 |
| B | 18:08–18:20 | 18:20–18:26 | 18:26–18:32 | 18:32–18:38 |
| C | 18:16–18:28 | 18:28–18:34 | 18:34–18:40 | 18:40–18:46 |

The visits require eighteen direct mentor-minutes. Two two-minute transitions, two minutes before the first visit and six after the last bring the booking to thirty. The cases are familiar from preparation. In this constructed timetable, each group has its recorded judgements and bounded question ready at the start of its visit; inspection and reply fit in six minutes. The mentor therefore need not attend each group’s preceding eighteen minutes. Check these conditions before relying on the schedule elsewhere. A longer question needs more provision or leaves a stated limit.

Each group has thirty active minutes without waiting for its mentor; the cohort spans 18:00–18:46. Confirm the relevant participants’ availability before offering this schedule. If everyone must leave at 18:30, A can finish but B and C cannot complete their personal returns; B’s mentor visit is interrupted and C misses its visit entirely. Obtain a compatible schedule or qualified capacity for the promised result, or report the limit. Longer movement, another group or further demand can also reopen feasibility. The planning assumption is that the existing coordination allowance covers confirming the starts. Include preparation, reading, exchange, return and correction in learner time. Price and learning outcomes require their own grounds.

Four initial fragments arrive without grounds. Prepared, permitted contrasts can preserve a Wednesday comparison while those learners complete their own grounds for personal application if feasible. Use the substitute for the work it supports. It cannot establish that the four learners supplied the missing grounds before the meeting. If a necessary subject method is unavailable, name the dependency. A later deadline alone cannot supply it.

#### HCD.27:5.2 - A missed conversation is not a missed file

One learner misses Wednesday but can read the cases and result. If the target is personal use of the relation, a supported individual comparison and Thursday feedback may supply the needed continuation. If the learner must explain under a peer’s challenge, the reading supplies information. For the missing exchange, use a compatible partner, time and qualified help where needed, or report the remaining limit. Retain completed preparation and include any added work and delay.

#### HCD.27:5.3 - Internal work and loss of a platform

An internal team has a short shared window during paid work and lacks permission to export project material to the programme platform. It uses the permitted internal source and local feedback arrangement. A separate outside exchange may use a public case that preserves the relation without exporting the project data.

If the platform becomes unavailable, identify the material and contact needed for the next action. Use an authorized alternative that preserves the required source version, permissions and prior responses when one is available. A restored file can supply the material. If the task needs a mentor or partner, establish whether a suitable person can supply the required interaction in time. Use HCD.7 or HCD.8 to assess or obtain that provision; report the remaining limit when it cannot be supplied. Continue unaffected individual work where useful.

### HCD.27:6 - Bias-Annotation

A common timetable can conceal missing inputs. Unlimited personal exceptions can exceed provider capacity. Use current entry evidence and finite windows. A late submission establishes its timing. A claim about a person’s preparation or capability needs evidence about that person and task.

### HCD.27:7 - Conformance Checklist

- Shared timing is justified by a needed learning contribution.
- For a proposed transfer, establish how the recipient can obtain and use the material. For a completed one, establish what reached the recipient and whether it was usable for the intended work in time. To claim personal use, examine what the learner did.
- Where selection or transformation is required, check whether it preserves the meaning and access conditions needed for the receiving use.
- Check peak demand against available provider and learner windows when qualifying feasibility.
- Identify feasible continuations for different entry needs, or the particular entry condition that remains unmet.
- For needed re-entry, preserve completed work and identify what the replacement can restore. Establish actual restoration when that is claimed.
- A substituted activity carries its changed learning and evidence limits.

### HCD.27:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

**Connect homework and a meeting by date alone.** Identify the material the meeting needs from the homework. For a completed episode, establish which part arrived and whether the meeting could use it.

**Everyone submits together, so the programme is coordinated.** Check the resulting service peak.

**The recording restores participation.** Determine which missing contribution it can supply.

**Personalisation without a boundary.** Compare preparation and recovery with finite support and an attainable result.

### HCD.27:9 - Consequences

A programme can preserve useful exchanges while supporting different personal continuations. Tracing a connection can uncover an unavailable input before dependent work begins. Coordination and recovery take effort. Sometimes the result is an adjusted window or promise, and sometimes it is a precise finding that the current promise cannot be met.

### HCD.27:10 - Rationale

Activities compose through usable results. Aligning a date without aligning what arrives can preserve the appearance of a programme while breaking its learning contribution. Tracing the needed result backward and its personal use forward exposes where to prepare, transform, support or resume the work.

### HCD.27:11 - SoTA-Echoing

The [official FROG account](https://wonderlab.gse.upenn.edu/projects/frog.html) supplies a concrete design line: results from individual asynchronous annotation can become material for synchronous group work. It describes how to arrange that transfer. A claim of causal advantage for the platform would require evidence about that effect. Sections 4.2–4.4 develop selection, usable return and recovery for the present HCD use.

The contact and rematching construction of [Zhang, Allon and Van Mieghem, draft 21 September 2015, §3.3](https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/30-Does-Social-Interaction-Improve-Service-Quality-Field-Evidence-from-Massive-Open-Online-Education.pdf) supports separating assigned contact from a completed exchange. HCD.7 supplies the developed provider-window comparison. Compared with calendar-only coordination, the method adds inspection of actual inputs; compared with fully separate programmes, it retains compatible sharing. Reconsider when preparation differences, service peaks or recovery costs outweigh the shared contribution. The worked timetable is a planning construction, not an empirical finding about paid adult education.

### HCD.27:12 - Relations

Use HCD.2 for a known person’s programme and HCD.28 when designing for a future audience. HCD.20 and HCD.21 can help assess arrangements and membership. Use HCD.22–HCD.25 for the relevant shared task or comparison. Use HCD.7 to establish usable support, and HCD.8 when the missing contribution must be sourced or built. HCD.9 and HCD.10 guide needed practice and correction. HCD.26 addresses shared work and HCD.14 an affected individual arrangement. Use Operations methods for service-wide scheduling or capacity.

### HCD.27:End

## HCD.28 - Construct and Revise a Whole Learning Product for a Future Audience

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner learning-product construction pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.28:0 - Use This When

Use this pattern to design or revise a learning offer for a future audience whose members may still be unknown, or to reconnect a programme, its material and its support. Start with the contribution learners will need to make in later work, the preparation they may bring and the conditions under which the product could be supplied.

A **whole learning-product account** connects the intended result to the entry conditions, subject content, learning tasks, materials, practice, feedback, observation and delivery it requires. It can describe a usable design, compare feasible variants or identify a missing connection. A complete small family of tasks may give the recipient enough to proceed. State which larger outcomes remain open. For each proposed route, identify its full burden and any unresolved dependencies.

The author can find a missing connection before producing more lessons or enrolling more learners. A subject method may lack a criterion, the material may fail to teach an available method, or the service may be unable to supply help in time. The account can support a development, offer or launch decision. Claims about demand, readiness and what participants learned require evidence for those claims.

Use an adequate existing product directly when it fits. For a defect in one material, see [HCD.19](#hcd19---evaluate-instructional-material-through-representative-reader-work-and-diagnose-its-repair). For programme comparison for a known person, see [HCD.2](#hcd2---compose-and-compare-human-capability-development-programmes-for-later-work). When the customer needs a work result, a competent provider may deliver it. A promise to develop the customer’s own contribution also requires an opportunity for the customer to learn.

#### HCD.28:0.1 - Working Terms

| Term | Meaning in this pattern |
| --- | --- |
| learning product | A bounded offer through which an audience can undertake specified learning work under stated entry and support conditions. A guide, course or supported practice arrangement can carry parts of the offer. |
| programme | The planned preparation, practice, feedback, correction and observation over time. Materials describe or support that work. Evidence from delivery shows which parts took place. |
| subject method | The way of performing the target-domain work, including the choices and conditions needed for that work. It can require skilled demonstration or situated judgement as well as a written account. |
| pedagogical companion | Material and activities that help learners acquire prerequisites and understand and practise an available subject method. Developing a missing rule for the subject work requires subject expertise. |
| whole learning route | A connected path from an attainable entry through the learning activity and any needed correction to the observable contribution the offer promises. |
| preparation branch | An alternative entry or preparation activity selected by a relevant difference in starting capability, access or support. It has a return to the whole task. |
| supply arrangement | Who or what can provide the materials, access, checking and recovery, under which permissions and in which time windows. Check promised availability against the actual conditions. |

### HCD.28:1 - Problem Frame

Before the audience members are known, the author can qualify a task, compare explanations, prepare a practice route and estimate support. A personal diagnosis or programme recommendation needs evidence about the person.

An explanation may teach calculation while the later task requires model selection. A learner may need help after the mentor has left. A successful group report may contain one learner’s judgement although other participants never made the judgement themselves. A self-service price may omit the time to read, practise, check and repair. In each case, examine how one part of the offer contributes to the work that follows.

To distinguish an instructional choice from an unresolved subject question, use your own qualified subject knowledge, a suitable existing result or the contribution of someone qualified to interpret the case. The design calls for competence in tasks, support and resource comparison. Use the applicable domain authority for an engineering, clinical or other professional judgement that requires it.

### HCD.28:2 - Problem

How can an author construct and compare an attainable learning offer for a future audience, connect its contributions into a usable whole, and revise the affected part when a subject, learning or supply defect appears?

### HCD.28:3 - Forces

| Force | Tension |
| --- | --- |
| Common offer and different entrants | Reusable content reduces repeated development, while differences in preparation or access can require different routes. |
| Competent account and acquisition | A precise method account can support competent use while leaving a novice unable to acquire the required operation. |
| Whole tasks and manageable effort | Whole tasks preserve meaning and selection, while missing prerequisites or excessive simultaneous demands can prevent useful practice. |
| Other people's contribution | Peers and providers can improve available reasoning or feedback while concealing the learner's missing contribution. |
| Content and medium | A medium can make an operation accessible while adding production, access and maintenance costs without changing learning. |
| Scale and support | More learners can share fixed development costs while increasing individual checking, peak demand and recovery work. |
| Early comparison and stronger claims | A constructed route can expose a defect before delivery, while actual learning, transfer and causal effectiveness require their own observations. |

### HCD.28:4 - Solution

#### HCD.28:4.1 - Bound the offer by work and meaningful entry differences

Describe the later tasks, the learner’s own contribution, the help allowed in those tasks and the errors that would defeat the result. State what preparation you expect and what evidence would support that entry assumption or distinguish entrants who need different work. People described as engineers or beginners may all calculate correctly while differing in model selection.

Identify what entrants may already know, what the offer must teach and what a permitted reference, tool or specialist can supply. If a tool makes the very choice the learner is meant to practise, change what the tool supplies or revise the learning claim.

Provide an alternative entry when preparation, access or support changes the needed work. An entrant who confuses units may need a short preparation task. An entrant who already selects models may need a different challenge or can omit that module. Identify an action or appropriate prior evidence for assigning the entry and where it leads next. A short diagnostic attempt may settle an uncertainty about preparation.

Treat assumptions about a future audience as conditional. For a known person, HCD.2 can use the feasible product or variants, their entry and support requirements, and their limits alongside evidence of that person’s starting performance, later work, participation, access and protected contributions.

#### HCD.28:4.2 - Obtain the subject contribution before repairing its teaching

Inspect a representative task and the available explanation or demonstration of competent work. When selection matters, inspect a nearby case where a change in conditions affects the choice. Establish whether the source supplies the judgement or operation the learning task requires.

| Finding | Next construction and usable return |
| --- | --- |
| An available method specifies the relevant selection, action and limits. | Use it as the subject basis. Preserve its scope and build teaching, practice and help for the declared preparation. |
| Competent practitioners can act, but a decisive choice remains implicit. | Use qualified demonstrations, examples or supervised work where they make the judgement available for learning. HCD.5:4.2.1 and HCD.6.1 help develop that work. If the missing operation or criterion still prevents the intended use, use A.3.1.MR to recover a candidate method. Use RMP.10 when the receiving question needs its larger evidence programme. |
| No qualified way of handling the required case is available. | Identify the missing subject relation, the intended use and what remains to be established for that use. Narrow or defer the unsupported part of the offer. When developing the missing method is part of the task, use Method Engineering or Research Method Practice or obtain the needed contribution. |
| The subject account serves a competent user, but the intended learner cannot recover or practise the operation. | Use HCD.5, HCD.6 or HCD.6.1 to develop the needed explanation, contrast, preparation or practice. Use HCD.19 when the question is what the material contributes. |
| Content and task are usable, but promised help or access is absent. | Identify the resulting limit. To make the offer usable, use HCD.7 to arrange available support or HCD.8 to obtain or build the missing contribution. Change the service within the applicable authority or take the unresolved change to the responsible provider. |

Several gaps can coexist. Even with a qualified subject criterion, a learner may still need a mentor in the feedback window. A contradictory explanation may still need correction after a mentor has been assigned.

Ask what the companion’s author would have to do. Choosing examples, ordering explanations, designing practice and withdrawing help as the learner gains capability are instructional work. Establishing the criterion for selecting the subject model is work on the subject method. An expert may use a concise account that leaves a novice without a way to learn the judgement.

#### HCD.28:4.3 - Construct the connections in one complete learning route

Work back from the intended result to the entry and contributions it requires. Then follow the proposed route from that entry. Use [HCD.5](#hcd5---select-human-capability-development-methods) to select how to develop a contribution the learner still needs, [HCD.6](#hcd6---design-representative-practice-tasks) to construct or assess the whole task, criterion, permitted help and variation, and [HCD.6.1](#hcd61---help-a-learner-discern-a-needed-distinction-in-practice) for a distinction the learner still needs to discern.

For each connection the route needs, identify what the first activity supplies and how the next can use it. The following examples illustrate different connections.

- Where learners must choose a model, a worked contrast can expose the condition that changes the choice. A later task can ask them to choose without a cue that gives the answer.
- If feedback concerns an attempt, the person giving it needs an interpretable judgement or performance. An earlier recorded attempt may supply it.
- When feedback is part of the route, it must reach the learner in time to use it. Give the learner grounds to correct or retain the response while the opportunity remains open.
- A later task can vary or preserve the condition relevant to the intended inference. To claim transfer, use a task and evidence that distinguish it from repeated performance under the original conditions.
- For a revision to affect the next use, the changed material or instruction must reach the participants who rely on it in time.

The [4C/ID account](https://www.4cid.org/about/) distinguishes whole learning tasks, support for non-routine reasoning, information used during routine action and additional practice on a component. Choose the contributions that make the whole learning task possible for the intended entrants.

Identify which contributions can overlap and which depend on an earlier result. Unit support can remain available during diagnosis. To assess independent model choice, preserve the choice before any cue that names the model reaches the learner. An appropriate existing task or provider result can already satisfy a dependency.

Use HCD.20 to compare or assess arrangements involving other learners and HCD.22 to construct or assess a shared task. A supported individual route can meet the complete promise. For shared work, identify the contribution others would need to provide and how learners could use it. For a delivered activity, establish which contributions participants supplied and, when the claim concerns uptake, what learners did with them.

When the route depends on interaction, select the contribution it needs. HCD.21 can help assess or arrange membership and contact. HCD.23 concerns exchange of explanations, HCD.24 judgement and revision through peer review, and HCD.25 comparison across projects and personal application. HCD.26 helps assess or regulate shared learning. HCD.27 connects personal preparation, shared occasions and recovery. Carry the applicable preparation, help and time conditions into the product assessment.

#### HCD.28:4.4 - Select the material and service forms for those connections

Choose a representation for the operation it enables. A table can support comparison of two measurements, a diagram can expose a relation, an animation can show relevant timing, and a simulator can let a learner choose an action and inspect its consequences. Judge each against the learning task and the cost and accessibility of the medium.

Identify the subject account, teaching companion, practice materials and service instructions even when they share a file or interface. Keep the subject criterion identifiable when an example or one of the materials changes. A reminder may cue a known operation. When learners still need to acquire that operation, identify a source, demonstration or practice through which they can learn it.

For a Guide or Slidement, use the Learning Product practice for instructional design and its presentation. For a course or mentoring service, establish the programme and the provider and delivery arrangements required for that service. SYSE.2 and SYSE.8 can help address questions about use and provision. For changes to assignments, capability or service operation, use an applicable decision, decide within your own authority or take the remaining question to the responsible organization or operations authority.

State what version of a case, answer basis or tool the task uses when a change would alter correctness or feedback. When the criterion changes, identify dependent examples, exercises, mentor guidance and interpretation of prior responses. When only access or timing changes, preserve unaffected subject content.

#### HCD.28:4.5 - Compare complete alternatives at a finite scale

For a comparison, use a common intended outcome, audience assumptions, assistance conditions, observation purpose and horizon, and identify relevant differences in learning support. Develop a less documented option far enough to assess it, and state any consequential difference in what the options can deliver. If the task is to assess one design, test its connections and burden against its requirements.

Estimate the learner’s search, orientation, preparation, participation, practice, correction and time waiting, along with authoring, production, provider preparation, delivery, checking, coordination, recovery and updates. Distinguish active and elapsed time and the work of each participant. Money, scarce expert time and displaced work can affect the comparison differently.

Count shared development once over the planned uses and recurring checks where they occur. Six minutes of help within a booked mentor session are part of that booking. If a peer supplies the help, count the peer’s time and establish whether it meets the need. Include tool charges alongside the work needed to use and check their output.

Alongside the totals, check peak demand. Find when the input for help will exist, which qualified provider can respond then and when the learner can use that response. Count movement or connection time and preserve each required personal action. Tomorrow’s mentor window cannot supply feedback needed today. If the window fails, consider another qualified provider, staggered starts, a changed task or a narrower offer as appropriate. State what each changes for learning or timing.

When a construction cannot meet the requirements, return the constraint and any surviving options. If a revised offer omits practice or checking the original outcome required, identify what the revised offer can still deliver.

#### HCD.28:4.6 - Exercise the whole route and separate what has been established

Use qualified materials and a walk-through or representative enactment to follow the proposed route and test whether its connections work together, reusing checks that already cover them. Check instructions, inputs, timing and allowed help. For a question about what readers can do with the material, use HCD.18 and HCD.19 with the relevant preparation and support. To report what real learners did, use observations of their work.

For a claim about a delivered activity, use the evidence that claim needs, such as entry conditions, first response, help received, feedback, a correction or reason for retaining the answer, or a later observation. Use HCD.11 for performance under specified conditions, HCD.12 for unfamiliar or new-source work, and HCD.13 for delay or dependence on support. Report material use, provider performance or the learner’s capability according to the evidence for each.

Use the finding to identify which connection needs attention. Repeated unsupported causal choices despite correct calculation warrant examining model selection and how it is taught. A single response can support a narrower finding about that attempt. Late feedback points to supply. Incompatible versions point to distribution. Change the affected connection when revision is warranted and retain the parts that still work. Use HCD.14 for development revision and HCD.16 for a changed claim about a method.

To attribute an improvement in learning to the product, use evidence from a research design that supports the causal comparison, obtaining more only if the intended inference needs it. Address the units receiving the intervention, interactions within or between groups, shared providers, comparison conditions, attrition, horizon and other plausible explanations where they affect the inference. A demonstration or a before-and-after difference can establish a narrower result.

#### HCD.28:4.7 - Return a construction that its recipient can use

Return the design, assessment or comparison the recipient needs. Identify the intended work and personal contribution, plausible entry and relevant branches, subject basis, connections among tasks, materials and support, burden and peak constraints. Report evidence, unresolved dependencies and the conditions that would change the conclusion.

Name a missing contribution in terms of the work it would enable. For example, a qualified pressure interpretation for two named cases can guide a decision to obtain or develop it. A usable design, a sufficient comparison or an established limit can complete the current task. Full production and launch require their applicable decisions. Use observations of delivery for claims about performance.

### HCD.28:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.28:5.1 - Future diagnosticians who calculate correctly but choose the wrong model

This constructed case supplies the planning assumptions for a module. Evidence from delivery would be needed to report learning or its improvement.

An author plans a module for 24 future technical diagnosticians. The audience hypothesis is that they can calculate energy per unit volume but may treat a rise in that ratio as proof of one cause. The later contribution is to name plausible rival explanations, choose an observation that distinguishes them, and recommend only the action the evidence supports. Safe case data and the subject answer basis come from a qualified domain contributor.

In the pump family from HCD.5 and HCD.6, power rises from 20 to 22.4 kW while flow stays at 100 m³/h. Energy per unit volume rises by 12%. The ratio alone leaves increased hydraulic resistance, changed efficiency and a measurement problem possible. The learning task is to identify an observation that distinguishes the live explanations or establish what remains open.

The author chooses the next work according to what the available basis supplies.

- If the expert’s account explains how a pressure observation distinguishes the models, use that basis to select or design a contrast and a choice task.
- If the expert’s choice is implicit, check whether a qualified demonstration or supervised task makes it learnable. If the rule itself remains missing and the product needs it, recover the criterion and test it against another case before presenting it as established.
- If the material states the relation but hides the relevant conditions, identify the material defect. For a repair, revise it and check the affected reader use.
- If a learner will need qualified help and no provider can supply it within the feedback window, identify that constraint. To deliver the outcome, arrange feasible help or revise the offer.

Plan a 90-minute core. Allow 20 minutes for the entry check and worked contrast, 10 for a first judgement, 30 for comparing reasons, 10 for a changed case, 15 for feedback and any needed correction, and 5 for a return plan. A 20-minute unit-support branch leads back to the whole diagnosis. Six entrants taking it add two learner-hours. The individual route below retains the core. The four-person route needs six more active minutes per learner for qualified help. These allowances can be checked in delivery.

In route A, each learner compares qualified reasons and can use individual subject help. In route B, four-person groups compare evidence under HCD.22 before an individual changed-case task. Use comparable outcomes and final assistance conditions. If the outcome requires responding to another person’s objection, check that A elicits it. If it does not, add an attainable exchange or report its narrower scope. For B, inspect which contrasts the group makes available.

For this comparison, allow six hours to qualify the common cases and two more for each route’s materials and provider preparation. At eight minutes per entrant, checking 24 initial responses takes 192 minutes. A plans 24 six-minute appointments, 144 minutes in bookable windows. B needs six six-minute group visits, 36 minutes of direct help. One mentor cannot provide these in a thirty-minute booking. In the feasible HCD.20:5.1 proposal, two mentors are booked from 11:00 to 11:30. Pairs of four-person groups start at 10:50, 11:00 and 11:10. Each group spends twelve minutes on initial explanations, six on help, twelve on second personal contributions and six on reconciliation.
